activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane, called chemiosmosis, and won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
story:
The trail behind the school cut along a creek, and Aaron had spread his notes across a flat rock like evidence at a trial nobody had asked him to defend. The exam was Monday. Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain: words he could recite but could not see, and Mr. Papadopoulos had made it clear that reciting would not be enough this time.

"Quiz me," he said.

Henry dropped his backpack in the dirt and sat on the root of a sycamore. "I'm not carrying your flashcards."

"You don't have to carry them. Just hold them." Aaron fanned the cards out, and Harper, arriving late with a bag of gas station pretzels, picked one up before he could stop her.

"'Where is the ATP made,'" she read. "Mitochondria. Even I know that."

"That's the question everyone gets right," Aaron said. "The question everyone gets wrong is how." He stood up and paced the length of the rock. "So glucose gets broken down, and the energy's supposed to end up in ATP, in the mitochondria. But my notes just say the chain 'powers ATP synthesis.' Powers it how. What's actually pushing."

Harper crumpled the pretzel bag into her jacket pocket. "Does it matter? The test is multiple choice."

"It matters because he'll write one question where the answer is the reason." Aaron heard how that sounded, like the jurisprudence of an appeal court where you had to argue principles and not just cite the law, and he didn't care. Half his grade was riding on arguing the principle.

They walked. The creek ran shallow over gravel, and a quarter mile up the trail it widened behind an old concrete weir, a low dam somebody had built decades ago to pool the water for irrigation. Henry stopped there, chewing a stem of grass, and pointed at the spillway with his chin.

"Look at that," he said. "All that water stacked up on the high side. It wants to fall. That's the whole thing, right there. You let it through a narrow gap and it turns a wheel."

Aaron looked at the water. Then he looked at his notes. On the page, the chain of protein complexes in the mitochondrial membrane, and next to one of them, an arrow with a plus sign and the word protons, pointing outward. He had copied that arrow without asking what it was for.

"Wait," he said. "The protons. The chain pumps protons across the membrane. They pile up on one side." He held up the notes so Henry could see the arrow. "Like water behind that dam."

"So let them fall back," Harper said. "Through whatever's in the membrane."

"The enzyme. ATP synthase." Aaron was talking fast now, almost tripping over the words. "If protons can only get back through that one spot, and falling back through it drives the enzyme, then the gradient is the power. Not some vague 'energy.' A difference, a buildup, like the water level here versus the water level down there." He crouched at the edge of the pool and put two fingers in, feeling the pressure of the held water against them, faint and constant.

Harper took her phone out. "Somebody must have figured this out first," she said, and typed. She went quiet in the way she did when she was actually reading instead of pretending to. Then she held the screen out.

Aaron read it twice. Peter Mitchell had proposed it in 1961, that cells make ATP using a proton gradient across a membrane. He'd won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

"There's a name for it," Harper said, scrolling. "Chemiosmosis."

"It sounds made up," Henry said.

"It sounds like the name of something people laughed at first," Aaron said. He read the years again. 1961 to 1978, seventeen years between the idea and the prize, and he thought of every answer he'd ever left blank because he wasn't sure. Mitchell had apparently been unsure for nearly two decades and kept going anyway. Not that Aaron was comparing himself. He was just noticing that certainty wasn't the thing he'd been told it was. In school they valorized the right answer, the clean fill-in, and here was the whole field of biology standing on a guess a man had made about a dam inside a cell, a guess so odd it took the rest of science a generation to catch up.

He said none of this out loud. He sat down on the concrete lip of the weir, took out a pencil, and drew it in the margin of his notes: a membrane like a long line, protons crowded above it, one channel through, ATP coming out the other side. Then he drew a little dam and an arrow between the two drawings.

"That's what I'll remember," he said. "Not the flashcards. This."

Harper looked over his shoulder. "You're going to draw a dam on the exam?"

"If the question is how, I'll draw a dam on the exam." He was smiling, but his hand had gone tight around the pencil. Because here was the part he couldn't fix by walking a trail: the rest of it, glycolysis, the exact order of the cycle, the parts where his notes said "then" and his brain said nothing. He had the principle now, the reason the machine ran, and he still might blank on the names of its gears. He could hold both of those facts at once, the understanding and the possible failure, without pretending either one canceled the other out.

"Thirty more minutes," Henry said, standing and brushing off his jeans. "Then I'm going home."

Aaron gathered the cards, squared them, and put them in his pocket with the folded notes. He looked once more at the pooled water, at the way it gathered all its quiet weight against the wall before it fell.

"One more question," he said, and dealt the top card to Harper. "Where's the ATP made?"

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
Aaron had folded the page into quarters so many times that the creases had gone soft, and still the schedule written on it made no sense to him. He sat on the low wall at the edge of the court with his sneakers dangling, watching Leland run suicides at the far end, each sprint dissolving into the next until the drill seemed interminable. On the page, Aaron had written Monday through Sunday and filled every line with something. Ball handling, shooting, conditioning, more conditioning. He had not left a single box empty, because empty felt like laziness, and laziness was the thing his father accused him of whenever the varsity list went up without his name on it.

"You're staring at that paper like it insulted your mother," Leland said, arriving at the wall with his shirt dark at the shoulders. He dropped down beside Aaron and reached for the water bottle before asking, which was how it had always been between them.

"It's my training plan. Mr. Dela Cruz wants it Friday. He said a week, so I gave him a week, but every day full." Aaron turned the page toward him. "Is that wrong?"

Leland squinted at it. "You've got Sunday as two-a-days. After six straight days."

"I can handle it."

"You couldn't handle the stairs after Tuesday's practice last week. I watched you take them sideways."

Aaron took the page back. The truth of it sat there in his own handwriting, seven crowded lines with no gap anywhere, and he could not find the argument against what Leland had said except that he wanted it to be otherwise. Wanting, he was beginning to suspect, was not a plan.

Aryana came out of the gym with a laptop under her arm and a protein bar she broke in half without ceremony, offering the larger piece to Aaron first. She had the strange habit of noticing who had eaten and who had not. "Dela Cruz's thing?" she said, nodding at the page. "Mine's done. He made us read the chapter in the coaching book first."

"The book's in the room past his office," Leland said. "The one with the broken blind. I had to sign it out like a library."

They walked there together, the three of them, through the corridor that smelled of floor wax and old rubber, and Mr. Dela Cruz was at his desk grading something, but he only pointed at the shelf and went back to his red pen, which Aaron understood as permission. The chapter was short. Aaron read it standing up while Aryana read over his shoulder, and it was there, in a paragraph between two diagrams, that he found the word he had been missing. He read the sentence twice.

"Periodized training," he said out loud, mostly to himself. "You split the season into cycles." He traced the diagram with one finger. "The smallest one is called a microcycle, and it usually lasts about one week."

"So your page is a microcycle," Aryana said. "That's all it is. One block."

"And the block has rest in it." Aaron flipped back a page, then forward again, checking that he had it right. "Rest is part of it. It's written in, not skipped."

"Which day do you cut?" Leland asked.

That was the harder question than it looked. Aaron had assumed that learning the system would tell him what to do, and instead it only told him the shape of what to do, which felt at first like a circumlocution, a long way around the simple instruction he had wanted, simple being rest less, work more, get better. But standing there with the book open, he understood that the system was asking him a different question than his father's voice asked. The voice asked how much he could survive. The system asked what his body could absorb, and those were not the same, and he could not yet prove which one he believed in, only that he had been living entirely inside the first one.

He took a fresh sheet from Mr. Dela Cruz's desk, mouthing sorry, and copied the week again with Sunday empty and a warm-up block penciled into every other day. He filled in the rest day last, deliberately, writing REST in capital letters as if it were a drill like any other, because on this page it was. Some part of him still resisted, still wanted to fill it, and he let that part stay rather than pretend it had left. He would find out in three weeks, when tryouts came, whether the empty box had cost him or saved him, and no diagram in any book could tell him that in advance.

Outside, the court was emptying, the light going long and orange across the far rim. Aaron folded the new page once, cleanly, and put it in his back pocket. Then he picked up the ball Leland had left on the free-throw line, spun it once in his hands, and shot from exactly where he stood.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together.
story:
The last box in Isla's room was labeled Miscellaneous, which she suspected was a polite word for things she could not decide about. She sat on the floor with her back against the mattress, since the bed frame was already in the truck downstairs, and held her phone against her ear while Alex talked about the parking situation at their old school, which was suddenly, unbearably interesting to both of them.

"You're doing the thing," Alex said. "Where you agree with me about nothing specific."

"I'm not equivocating. I'm tired. There's a difference."

"It's been three days, Isla. You moved forty minutes away. That's not even a time zone."

It was forty minutes without traffic, which was a way of saying never, and they both knew it, and neither of them said so. She could hear Aubrey in the background at Alex's end, arguing with someone about whether phylogeny counted as a vocab word for the bio final, and Isla realized she was memorizing the sound of them the way you memorize a page you're about to turn.

"Call me when you unpack," Alex said. "Or don't unpack. Just call."

Afterward she opened her laptop, which still remembered the Wi-Fi password from the old house, and searched how long it takes to make close friends, because she wanted a number she could plan around, something with edges. The first result was a study. Jeffrey Hall, 2018: he'd estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together. She read it twice, then did the arithmetic on the back of a packing slip. If she saw a new person for an hour a day, every single day, no sick days, no weekends off, that was more than half a year. More than 200 hours, and that was just to arrive. She and Alex had been building for eleven years, and she had just loaded the whole structure onto a truck.

She was still holding the packing slip when her mother came up with two mugs and handed one over without comment, which was its own kind of conversation. "The neighbors brought cookies," her mother said. "The woman from across the street. Ms. Gill. She asked whether you were diurnal or a night owl, because apparently that determines which window gets the good morning light."

"She said diurnal?"

"She said a bunch of words. I liked her." Her mother sat on the stripped mattress. "There are raisin ones too, if you hate chocolate."

Isla took a chocolate one. The mug was warm and the cookie was dry and someone had carried both across a street to a house with an empty porch swing, and she felt something loosen in her chest that she did not want to examine yet. "Mom. Did you have friends when you moved here? The first time, I mean. Before I was born."

Her mother looked at the window, where the good light was already fading. "I had one, within a year. And I lost whole afternoons to a woman who turned out to be cruel about my accent. So I don't know what to tell you. Both things were true."

Downstairs, the doorbell rang. Isla answered it expecting the movers, but it was Alex, still in the school parking lot sticker on the windshield, holding a plastic bag. "Aubrey's car," Alex said. "We skipped last period. Don't make it a thing." In the bag was Isla's spare hairbrush, forgotten under the bleachers since September, and a spiral notebook Aubrey had filled over the past three days with everyone's handwriting in it, a page per person, predictions about the new town.

Isla flipped through it on the porch steps while Alex picked the raisins out of a cookie. On Aubrey's page, in the margin, small: 200 hours is nothing, we already banked like 5,000, you can't spend them all at once. Isla read it and felt the twist land somewhere between her ribs. They had done the same search. They had done the same arithmetic and come out with a different total.

She handed the notebook back. "It's more than 200 hours," she said. "To start over. That's the actual number."

"Then we start the clock," Alex said, and took a bite of the cookie, raisin side first, deliberately, the way they used to during finals week, and Isla laughed and waved at Ms. Gill, who was watering her garden in the last of the light.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs, while an endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter.
story:
Nevaeh set her laptop on the cafe table between Asha's untouched hot chocolate and Kaia's physics binder, opened her document, and discovered that her notes were gone. Not deleted; she scrolled and found them, all fourteen, crowded onto the final page after the bibliography, numbered and patient, like passengers herded to the wrong end of a train.

"I had them at the bottoms of the pages," she said. "I spent an hour on that."

Asha leaned over, earrings swinging. "An hour on what? They're just little numbers."

"They're not just numbers." Nevaeh scrolled up to page four, where the number three floated at the end of a sentence about lead pipes in Roman aqueducts. "Mr. Chea said the whole point is that a reader can check you. He's on sabbatical this term, so nobody's even checking me, and I still have to do it right."

Kaia pulled her binder closer as a woman with a stroller eased past their table toward the counter. "What's the difference where they live? They're in the document."

"That's the thing. I don't know if there's a difference." Nevaeh clicked through the word processor's menus, found a settings panel, and stared at it. The software offered her a choice it had apparently already made without asking her: it had gathered every note onto the last page. Somewhere in her memory, Mr. Chea's voice from last spring, before he left, said something about footnotes that she had not written down.

She opened the style guide the librarian had photocopied for her, the one folded into her backpack's front pocket since September. The pages smelled like the toner of the school copier. She ran her finger down the table of contents, past sections on margins and titles, and found a short entry with two words she had never properly separated: footnote and endnote.

"There," she said, and read it twice, slowly, because the first time the words slid past her the way numbers did when she was tired.

"What," Asha said, not really a question, just permission to keep talking.

"A footnote appears at the bottom of the page where the reference occurs," Nevaeh said. "An endnote collects the same kind of note at the end of the paper or chapter." She said it out loud once more, quieter, testing the weight of the two words against each other. What she had built, without knowing it, was an endnote system. What she had wanted, or thought she wanted, was footnotes.

"So your notes at the end are an endnote," Kaia said. "That's a thing that exists. Somebody named it. So it's allowed."

"It's a thing that exists," Nevaeh said. "Whether it's allowed is a different question." She turned her cup of tea without drinking it. The style guide told her where each kind belonged but not which one Mr. Chea's assignment required, and the assignment sheet, which she pulled from her backpack and flattened against the table, said only "notes and bibliography in a standard citation style." It did not say footnote. It did not say endnote. It assumed she would know, and she had not known, and now she knew half of something.

The cafe's espresso machine sighed behind the counter. Asha stole a sip of Kaia's hot chocolate while Kaia pretended not to see, the way she had been doing since tenth grade.

"Here's what I actually think," Nevaeh said. She copied the sentence from the style guide into her notes document, then sat back. "The software defaults to endnotes. That means endnotes are normal to somebody, probably to a lot of somebodies, probably to whole presses and journals. So it can't be wrong in general. But footnotes are on the page where the reference occurs, and that matters for my argument, because half my evidence is about how close the pipes were to the drinking water. If the reader has to flip to the end, the distance gets bigger. I want the note right there under the sentence, where you can't avoid seeing it."

"That's weirdly persuasive," Asha said. "You're arguing for the placement of your notes like they're evidence."

"They are evidence. Everything's evidence if it's doing work." Nevaeh looked at the settings panel again. There was a radio button, small and gray, that would send every note back to the bottom of its own page. Her cursor hovered over it. She thought about how the paper had looked both ways, and how she could not quite say one was dishonest and the other honest, only that one placed the proof where the claim lived and the other archived it. She decided that the assignment sheet's silence meant she had to choose, and that choosing, and being able to say why, was probably the part Mr. Chea would have cared about, on sabbatical or off it.

She clicked the button. Fourteen numbers slid backward through the document, one to each page, settling under their sentences like birds returning to ledges. Page four now carried its small numbered three at the bottom, directly beneath the pipes and the water and the sentence it served.

"There," she said. "Now read my second paragraph and tell me if you believe me."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: An argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false; validity depends only on the argument's form, not on whether the premises are true.
story:
The resolution on the board read: This house would ban unpaid internships, and Charlotte had four minutes to demolish the affirmative case she had spent a week building. She stood at the podium in Ms. Iyer's classroom, three desks pushed aside for the tournament practice, and waited for Nathan to finish scribbling his rebuttal.

Nathan argued that unpaid internships exploit students whose families cannot subsidize them, and that if a system depends on free labour, the system deserves to fail. It was clean, and it was passionate, and Charlotte had prepared eighteen statistics against it. But as he spoke, she found herself watching Diana in the second row, mouthing along with him like a choir director, and she remembered something from a night that had nothing to do with internships.

It was October, and the three of them had habituated themselves to the coffee shop on Delancey after practice, same corner table, same chipped mugs, until the staff stopped asking what they wanted. Diana had been stirring cold foam into a puddle and announced, with great ceremony, that all dragons breathe fire, that Smaug is a dragon, and that therefore Smaug breathes fire. Nathan had thrown a sugar packet at her. You can't prove something with dragons, he said. Dragons aren't real. And Diana, unhurt, even delighted, had leaned across the table and said, "It's valid anyway. Valid means the premises can't all be true while the conclusion's false." Charlotte had laughed at her then, because it sounded like a trick, like being right by cheating. But Diana had drawn it out on a napkin, arrows and brackets, and said the form held even if nothing in it existed. Validity, she had said, lives in the shape, not the content. Charlotte had kept the napkin in her binder for a week, folding and unfolding it, wondering whether an argument could be a kind of container, strong or leaky regardless of what you poured into it.

"The member for the affirmative," Charlotte began, and her voice came out steadier than she felt, "has told us that if a system depends on free labour, it deserves to fail." She let the sentence sit. Then she asked the room, gently, almost curiously, whether they had noticed the shape of it. If this, then that. A conditional. And conditionals, she said, could be perfectly sound in form while resting on a premise that wobbles. She did not say the premise was false. She said she wanted to test it. Suppose, she offered, that some systems depending on free labour do not fail but mutate into something worse than failure, something that survives by habituating everyone involved to not noticing the cost. What did "deserves to fail" mean then?

Nathan's head came up. He had expected the statistics, the wage data, the class-action citations she had been waving around all week. He had prepared, she could see, for a war of numbers. Instead she was asking him a question about the interior of his own sentence, and his rebuttal notes, dense with counters she had never actually argued, sat useless in front of him.

Ms. Iyer, timing from the back with her phone face down on the desk, said nothing, but Charlotte caught her small nod, the kind that meant the teacher was watching something develop rather than judging it. Diana was no longer mouthing along. Her pen had stopped above her notebook, hovering.

He recovered enough to say that whether a system mutates or fails was empirical, a question for evidence, not for logic. And Charlotte agreed, which visibly unsettled him, because debaters were trained to never agree, to hold the line and be intransigent even when the line was drawn in sand. But she said agreement out loud anyway. Yes, she said, the truth of his premise was an empirical matter. What she wanted to separate was the two questions people kept collapsing: whether his reasoning held together, and whether the world it reasoned about was the actual world. An argument could have one without the other. You could follow the arrows on the napkin and still walk off a cliff if the first box was drawn in the wrong place.

The four minutes ran out mid-sentence, and she stopped, and in the quiet after, before Ms. Iyer could call the next speaker, Diana raised her hand as though this were still a class and not a scrimmage. "You stole my napkin," she said. "I want it on record that you laughed at me for that napkin."

"Assessment," said Ms. Iyer, "after we hear the negative summary." But she was smiling at her phone, and outside the window the parking lot was filling with cars for the afternoon session, and Nathan was crossing out half his notes. He looked up at Charlotte with the particular expression of someone rewriting in real time. "Same form, wrong world," he said, half to himself, testing it. "That's going to be brutal in the actual round."

Charlotte slid her index cards, all eighteen statistics untouched, back into her binder. "Ask me a conditional," she said. "Any one you want. I've got a whole box now."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Many people prefer $50 now over $100 in a year, yet prefer $100 in six years over $50 in five, a preference reversal called present bias.
story:
Mr. Goldberg's mentorship meetings happened in the community center's back room, which smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and which I attended every second Thursday because I was a serious person with long-term goals. I want that on the record. Nour came too, though she claimed it was only for the free printer access, and that afternoon she was feeding a worksheet through the machine while I laid out my proposal at the table by the window, where the low boreal light of a February afternoon came in sideways and made everything look like evidence in a case I intended to win.

The proposal was this: the youth council had sixty dollars in its account, and I wanted forty of it now for a launch event, posters and a speaker and a table at the winter fair. Mr. Goldberg had mentioned, vaguely, that if a project survived its first year, the neighborhood association would likely fund it properly the following winter. I had done the arithmetic on the bus. Forty now, or a real budget later. I was, as I have said, a serious person, so obviously I had chosen the patient route and was merely presenting it for approval.

"I like the spine of it," Mr. Goldberg said, tapping the page. "The city's new ordinance on fair vendors actually helps you, no permit fee for youth tables under the program. Saves you fifteen dollars you'd otherwise reify as a problem." He smiled at his own sentence. "But you're spending the reserve down to nothing. What happens in March when the rebooking fee comes due?"

"That's the interesting part," Nour said, coming back from the printer with the warm page still in her hand. "Ethan did a survey for econ. Watch this." She flipped the worksheet toward me. "Same question I gave you on Tuesday. A hundred dollars in a year, or fifty right now. What did you put?"

"Fifty right now," I said, because I had, and because I am honest. "Obviously. A year is a year."

"And then question two. Fifty in five years or a hundred in six."

"A hundred in six," I said. "That one's not even close."

Nour turned to Mr. Goldberg, who had leaned back with the expression of a man watching a nature documentary he'd already seen. "Same guy. Same numbers. He takes the fifty now, but for the far-out ones he's suddenly patient." She pointed the worksheet at me like a subpoena. "It's called present bias," she said. "That's the word for it."

"That survey was a sample of one," I said. "It doesn't prove anything about my actual decisions, which are, as demonstrated by my proposal, extremely far-sighted." I looked down at the proposal as I said this, at the line where I'd crossed out "wait for the association funding" and written "launch now, momentum matters," and I confess that for a moment the two versions of me, the one on the worksheet and the one at the table, sat on opposite sides of my head and refused to make eye contact. It was possible, I allowed internally, that I was not a patient person who occasionally took surveys, but an impatient person who had built an entire personality out of the far-off questions.

Mr. Goldberg said nothing, which was his way of saying a great deal. He got up and rinsed his cup at the sink, leaving the tap running a beat too long, letting the room be quiet around my proposal. I thought about March. I thought about the rebooking fee, which was not hypothetical, which was twenty dollars, and which the me of eleven months from now would have to pay with money the me of today was about to spend on posters.

"Here's what stays uncertain," I said finally, mostly to the window. "Maybe momentum is real. Maybe an event now builds something the association would never fund cold. I can't actually know that. But the fifty-now part, the part where I shortchange next year's Ethan because he feels like a stranger, that part I can see plain."

Nour sat down across from me and slid the worksheet back to my side of the table. "So rewrite it. Twenty now, keep the reserve, and apply for the real money for year two."

I took out my pen. Mr. Goldberg turned off the tap and sat back down, and outside the light had gone from boreal gold to the flat gray that means snow is coming, and I drew one line through the budget and started a second column. "Also," I said, without looking up, "next Tuesday you're giving me the survey again, and this time I want to see whether I've gotten any smarter."

"Fifty bucks says you haven't," Nour said.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In 2025, US union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404, compared with $1,174 for workers who were not union members, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
story:
Mr. Murphy had taped a yellowed photograph above the whiteboard, men in caps holding signs outside a mill, and he stood beside it with his arms folded while the third-period class settled. Jayden slid into his seat two minutes late, smelling faintly of the grocery store's produce section, where he had restocked until eleven the night before. His hands still ached from lifting crates of cantaloupe. Mr. Murphy marked the tardiness with a look rather than a word, and began the unit on the industrial era, on strikes and contracts and the long argument over what an hour of a person's life ought to cost.

Halfway through the period Mr. Murphy set them a question for discussion: whether a contract negotiated by a group could be fair to someone who never signed it. Graeme, who sat by the window, raised his hand first. Graeme worked at the Foodway on Route 9, and he had opinions about everything, delivered with the practiced elocution of someone who had been on the debate team since freshman year. "If the deal is good, everyone benefits," Graeme said. "If it's bad, everyone's stuck with it. That's the trade."

Jayden said nothing, though his mind was not quiescent. He worked at the Value Mart across town, nonunion, and last week Graeme had shown him a pay stub outside the gym, almost casually, the way boys show each other things they pretend not to be proud of. Graeme's stub, and Jayden's own, sat side by side in Jayden's memory now like two arguments. He had looked the numbers up that night on his phone, on the Bureau of Labor Statistics page, and found that in 2025 union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404, compared with $1,174 for workers who were not union members. Two hundred and thirty dollars a week, roughly. Jayden had done that math twice, then a third time, as if repetition might shrink it.

Aiyana, who wanted more than anything to be the youngest shop steward her store had ever elected, leaned across the aisle toward him. "You could ask about it, you know," she said under the discussion noise. "Your manager. Whether there's ever been a vote." She worked weekends at a warehouse where her mother had organized years ago, and she spoke about unions the way other people spoke about family recipes, with inherited certainty. "Or you could talk to the UFCW rep who comes by Foodway Tuesdays. He's not scary. He just hands out cards."

"Mr. Murphy," Graeme called out, drawing the class back, "can a company just fire everyone for trying?" Mr. Murphy turned the question around, patient as a river stone. "What do your textbooks say about the law?" He would not litigate the matter from the front of the room; he made them build the case themselves, pulling the National Labor Relations Act apart clause by clause until the room understood, in a slow collective way, that the right to bargain together was written down somewhere, that it had not arrived by kindness.

That was the part Jayden kept turning over after the bell. The right existed. The numbers existed. What did not exist was anything simple connecting the two to his own Tuesday nights, his closing shifts, the way his manager scheduled him until eleven and opened him at seven whenever someone quit. After school he stood in the Value Mart break room with Aiyana's words in his pocket and asked the manager, a tired woman named on her badge only as Doreen, whether the store had ever held a vote. She looked at him for a long moment. "Once, before you were born," she said. "It didn't take. People were scared, and the ones who weren't scared moved away." She handed him a broom.

He swept aisle six thinking about fear and arithmetic, how the second could be measured and the first could not. On Thursday he found Graeme at his locker and told him, flatly, the numbers, the medians, exactly as the page had given them, and Graeme nodded and said, "Yeah, but my union dues, man, they're not nothing either," which was true and which Jayden had no answer for, and which somehow made the whole thing more real than the statistics had. Graeme wanted the win to be clean. Jayden was beginning to suspect it never would be.

He did fill out one of Aiyana's cards, though, and folded it into his wallet behind his learner's permit, where it made a faint rectangle he could feel through the leather. He did not hand it in. He told himself he was waiting until he understood the dues, the meetings, the slow machinery of it, and that was partly true. On Friday Mr. Murphy asked him to stay a moment, said only, "Good question you asked Wednesday," and handed back Jayden's essay with a mark that surprised them both. Walking out past the photograph of the men with their signs, Jayden touched his wallet once, briefly, like checking for a key.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area under the curve y equals x squared, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, is exactly one third.
story:
The house smelled of vinegar again, because Grandmother had twelve jars of cabbage fermenting on the counter and refused to move them to the cellar. Leo set his graph paper on the kitchen table between the jars and the window, where the light was good, and pinned down the corner that kept curling.

The assignment had come from Mr. Villanueva on Friday: estimate the area under a curve without calculus, then, if you already knew some calculus, check your answer. Leo had texted Gurnoor about it on the bus. Gurnoor had written back, "just count squares, that's the whole assignment," and then, a minute later, "my grandfather used to do this on actual paper, he says." Leo had not answered. Counting squares seemed beneath the three weeks of integrals they had done, and at the same time he did not trust himself to count.

He drew the axes first, then the curve, y equals x squared, from 0 to 1, plotting a few points and connecting them with the careful slowness his drafting teacher would have approved. The curve rose slowly at first and then steeply, so that near the right edge it nearly ran off the box. Between it and the bottom of the square, the region he needed looked small, dark with pencil shading, like an archipelago of partial squares along a coastline.

Counting was worse than he had expected. A full square inside the region was easy, but the boundary squares were cut at every angle the parabola could invent, and Leo had to judge halves and thirds and eighths by eye. He marked each one with its fraction, then added them in the margin. He got 0.31 the first time and 0.34 the second time, and the difference bothered him more than either number. He drew the whole thing again on a fresh sheet, using a finer grid he ruled himself, ten divisions per unit instead of five. The finer grid gave him more boundary, not less, but the fractions were smaller, and the total came to 0.332, with a second count of the same sheet giving 0.328.

The integral was one line. He wrote it out on the back of the first sheet, the antiderivative of x squared, evaluated at 1 and at 0, and the subtraction. The answer was exactly one third. He looked at the decimal he had written under it, 0.333 repeating, and then at his two hand counts, which bracketed it the way a hand brackets something it cannot touch. He had expected the check to feel like a judge's gavel. Instead it felt quieter, like being told a secret his own counting had already almost whispered.

"So what is it," Grandmother said, setting a jar down beside his elbow without asking. She read upside down, which Leo had never gotten used to.

"One third exactly," he said. "From zero to one. The area under that curve."

"One third of what?"

"Of the whole square. Of one unit by one unit."

She looked at the shaded region, then at the jars fermenting along the counter, and said that in her opinion everything worth knowing was a fraction of something larger, and went back to the stove. Leo did not argue. The question he actually cared about was not hers anyway. What he wanted to know was whether the counting had been a waste of three days, an exercise for people destitute of better tools, or whether Gurnoor's grandfather had been right to do it on paper for decades. He thought about Gurnoor's "just count squares," said with such certainty, and about Mr. Villanueva, who had assigned both methods instead of either one, and had said nothing at all about which mattered.

Leo took out his phone and photographed the two sheets side by side, the shaded grid and the single line of symbols, and sent them to Gurnoor with no caption. Then he turned the finer grid back toward the window, picked up his pencil, and ruled out a third version, twenty divisions per unit, along the curve's steep right side where the boundary was hardest, while the cabbage ticked softly in its jars.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream is a warm ocean current that flows out of the Gulf of Mexico through the Florida Straits and north along the east coast of the United States.
story:
Claire had taped the ocean current map to the refrigerator with two magnets shaped like lobsters, which felt appropriate, since the map was mostly ocean and the lobsters were mostly claws. Her presentation was at nine the next morning, eleven minutes long, on how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe, and so far her working theory was that the ocean did something and Europe got warmer, which would not survive even a friendly audience.

At the kitchen table Fletcher sat with his chin on his fist, the sullen posture of a boy who had been promised snacks and delivered rice cakes. "You could just memorize a paragraph," he said. "People do it every day. Nobody checks."

"Ms. Lindqvist checks." Claire uncapped a marker. "She asked Devon last week why the sky was blue and he said 'molecules' and she made him sit down mid-sentence. Mid-sentence, Fletcher. The man never recovered."

Kohl arrived through the back door without knocking, the way he had since they were nine, carrying a bag of gummy worms like a diplomatic offering. He divided them, gave Fletcher first pick as compensation for the rice cakes, and leaned over the map. "Okay, so where's this famous stream? I want to see the celebrity."

Claire put her finger on the map. She had marked it in yellow highlighter earlier, after checking it three times against the museum's website, because she had gotten it wrong once already and the wrongness still itched. "It starts here," she said, dragging her fingertip slowly across the vinyl, "in the Gulf of Mexico. Then it squeezes through the Florida Straits, all these little islands there, and then it goes north along the east coast of the United States. Like this. Up the whole edge." Her finger stopped somewhere off New England, hovering over a swirl of blue arrows. "And after that, apparently, it heads across to Europe. That's the part I keep fumbling."

"That's the part that's the whole point," Fletcher said, through a gummy worm. "You've described a river and then said 'and magic happens.'"

"It's not magic, it's warm water." As soon as she said it she heard how it sounded, and Fletcher's eyebrows confirmed. Warm water, traveling north, arriving at cold places. She had been thinking of the map as a picture, a static thing to recite, the way you memorize a bus route. But the word "current" was doing actual work. A current moved. It carried things, the way a river carried a leaf, the way the radiator in the hallway carried warmth from the furnace to her cold bedroom all the way at the end of the hall. "Okay," she said slowly. "Okay okay okay."

"She's doing the triple okay," Kohl said to Fletcher. "Last time she triple-okayed, she reorganized the entire pantry."

"Which improved everyone's life," Claire said, but she was already pacing the kitchen, marker uncapped, gesturing at the refrigerator like a weather reporter with a grudge. "The water picks up heat down south, in the Gulf. It flows north along the coast, it crosses the ocean, and it arrives at northern Europe still carrying some of that warmth. Europe doesn't get it from nothing. It gets delivered." She stopped. "London is farther north than most of Canada, did you know that? People never believe that."

"That's because it's insane," Fletcher said.

"It's true, I looked it up, it's on the list." She tapped her notebook, where she kept a running list of facts that seemed fake but weren't, a collection she had started in seventh grade and never told anyone about, except both of them knew, because they read it when she wasn't looking.

Kohl was frowning at the map in his particular way, the one that meant he had found a crack in something. "But Claire. If warm water shows up in the north, doesn't the north cool it eventually? And doesn't the water have to come back? Where does it go after?"

Claire opened her mouth. She closed it. She looked at the map, at the arrows she had confidently yellowed, and had to admit, to the room and to herself, that she did not know. There was a whole system under the arrows, deep water, return flows, things called gyres, a word she had seen in her reading and not yet earned. She could explain the delivery without explaining the return trip. "I don't know," she said. "Honestly. I know the part I highlighted and I don't know the rest of it yet."

Fletcher, who had been waiting all evening for an opening like this, spread his arms. "Then say that. Tomorrow, up there, just say 'this is what I know, and this is where it stops.'"

"Ms. Lindqvist will fail me."

"Ms. Lindqvist will adopt you. She loves that stuff. She once gave Devon extra credit for saying 'I don't know' and then looking it up in front of everybody." Fletcher stood and pointed at the fridge with the gravity of a lawyer presenting evidence. "You've got the path, you've got the start, the straits, the coast, the crossing. That's a real thing. Don't pretend it's everything and it might actually be something."

Claire sat back down and pulled the notebook toward her. On a fresh page she wrote what she knew in a tight block: out of the Gulf of Mexico, through the Florida Straits, north along the east coast of the United States, across, warm water, northern Europe warmer than it should be. Then, underneath, in smaller letters, she wrote the honest part: where it goes after, and how it keeps going, still a mystery to me. It was not the encapsulation she had planned, not a tidy box with a bow, but a box with one side left open on purpose, so the question could breathe. She read it over twice and found she liked it better that way, the way a joke you can't fully land stays funnier than one you explain.

She looked up. "Eleven minutes is too long for what I have."

"Pad it with the London thing," Kohl said.

"Everyone pads with the London thing," Fletcher said. "It's the gummy worm of geography facts." He held up an empty bag as evidence, shook it once, and dropped it in the trash.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Arabic newspapers across many countries are written in Modern Standard Arabic rather than local spoken dialects, so one written form serves readers in different regions.
story:
Eva had promised herself she would be fluent enough to read a whole newspaper article by the time first semester started, and now the article sat in front of her in the school library, refusing to cooperate. The paper was a copy of an Arabic daily that Mr. Qureshi had brought back from a conference, folded to page eleven, where a story about a port expansion ran alongside a photograph of cranes. She had two weeks before the heritage language placement test, and her grandmother's kitchen-table Arabic, learned over a decade of summers, was proving to be a different animal from the thing printed on the page.

"It looks like what my grandmother says," Eva said, sliding the paper toward Maksim, "but it doesn't sound like her."

Maksim leaned over the table without touching it. He was here for chemistry, his notes fanned out beside a highlighted diagram, but he had been watching her mouth the same paragraph for twenty minutes. "So read it like her."

She tried. The first sentence came out in the cadence of her grandmother's kitchen, the vowels loose and Egyptian, and halfway through, something caught. A word she knew, but wearing different clothes. Then another. "See, that's the problem. Half of it is familiar and half of it is like a stranger wrote it with my grandmother's dictionary."

Tayla arrived with a granola bar and the particular energy of someone who had finished her homework during lunch. She dropped into the third chair. "Deadline check. Two weeks. What's the test actually going to make you do?"

"Read a short article out loud and summarise it in English. In front of somebody." Eva flattened the page with her palm. "I can summarise fine if I can read it. That's the part that's killing me."

Tayla took the paper and turned it upside down, as though that might help. "What if you just memorise the article? Get one from a newspaper, drill it, hope they pick something similar."

"That's not reading," Eva said. "That's theatre."

"It's strategy," Tayla said.

Maksim tapped the masthead with his pencil. "My uncle reads these. He's from Jordan, and he says everyone from Morocco to Dubai reads the same papers. One written Arabic for the whole region, no matter how differently they talk at home."

Eva sat back. The sentence landed somewhere between insult and relief. She thought of her grandmother saying that the radio never spoke like people, and how Eva had assumed this was a complaint, some private stubbornness about modern things. It had not occurred to her that the writing itself belonged to a different register, a shared formal language laid over dozens of spoken ones. Her kitchen Arabic was not a lesser version of the newspaper. It was one voice in a crowd, and the newspaper was speaking to all of them at once.

"Okay," she said slowly. "So when I read this out loud, I'm not reading it wrong. I'm reading it in the wrong accent for the job."

"You're reading it like Cairo," Maksim said. "The paper is from somewhere else. Or from nowhere."

Tayla was already pulling up something on her phone. "There's a clip. News anchor. Listen." The phone played a woman's voice, measured and formal, every ending crisp. Eva listened, then read the first sentence again, trying on the new rhythm the way she would try on a coat in a shop, checking the shoulders. It fit strangely. It fit.

The clock over the returns desk said the library closed at six, and it was already ten past five. Mr. Qureshi came through on his rounds, collecting stray pencils, and paused at their table. "Page eleven still holding your attention?"

"The port article," Eva said. "They're going to monetize the expanded terminals, there's a whole paragraph on it."

"And can you give me the summary?"

She took a breath. The story was about capacity, about who paid for the dredging, about a guarantee the company had demanded from the government before it would build, an indemnity against losses if the harbor's friable seabed shifted again and the new berths silted up. She said all of this in English, halting once at the indemnity clause and working around it, and Mr. Qureshi nodded, not warmly, just enough.

"Now the first paragraph. In Arabic, out loud."

She read it. Not in her grandmother's voice, not in the anchor's either, somewhere in between, a third accent that might not exist anywhere but at this table. Two words she guessed at, one she got wrong and corrected from context, and the sentence closed itself with a click she could almost hear.

"Again," Mr. Qureshi said. "Sixty seconds."

She read it again. Tayla's phone timer ran. At the end, Maksim said, "Faster."

"What I still don't know," Eva said, folding the paper along its old crease, "is whether the test wants the anchor or whether they'd take my grandmother. I'm going to practise both. One for the examiners, one for her." She tucked the newspaper into her bag, next to the chemistry notes Maksim was still shoving into his backpack, and the lights over the far shelves began their slow blink toward closing.

"Tomorrow, same table," Tayla said. "Bring the paper."

"I'm bringing the whole edition," Eva said.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: If two countries give up exactly the same amount of one good to make the other, neither has a comparative advantage, and Ricardo's model predicts no gain from specializing.
story:
Cameron had told the manager he was good with numbers, and until tonight the register had agreed. He counted the drawer at the start of his shift at the hardware store, served eleven customers, and counted again at closing, and now there was a twenty missing, and he was standing very still in the fluorescent light trying to decide whether to tell Ms. Hu before she found it herself.

The honest thing, he kept thinking, was to say it right away. But honest in which direction? If he said nothing, she might think the drawer was never short, or she might think he'd taken it, and both of those outcomes began with him keeping his mouth shut, which felt, in the moment, exactly like guilt. He ruminate on this too long, turning the same small decision over the way you turn a key that might not fit the lock, while Ms. Hu locked the front doors and Laurent swept around him with the patience of someone paid by the hour.

"You're doing that econ homework during breaks again," Laurent said, nodding at the textbook wedged beside the roll of quarters. "You're like an ascetic. No phone, no snacks, just graphs."

"Somebody has to pass the test Monday." Cameron pulled the book out now, glad for the excuse to look somewhere other than the drawer. The problem had been bothering him since four o'clock. Two countries, cloth and wine, and he'd worked the opportunity costs twice on the back of a receipt. Country A gave up exactly the same amount of one good to make the other as Country B did. Same ratio, both sides, all the way down. And the answer key in the back of the book said trade would not help them, that there was no reason for either one to specialize, and Cameron had written "printing error" in the margin because he didn't believe it.

He texted Amelia, who was better at econ than he was and worse at answering quickly. He got the drawer question, he typed. Both countries give up the same amount. Why no gain? He watched the message sit there, one grey checkmark, the way his worry about the twenty sat there too, unanswered.

Ms. Hu came down the aisle with the deposit bag. "Cameron, how did we do tonight?"

"Fine," he said. The word came out before he could judge it, and he heard himself say it the way you hear a door close behind you. "Steady."

She looked at him for a second longer than steady required. Ms. Hu ran the store with a kind of judicious calm, never accusing anyone of anything, which was somehow worse, because it left you alone with the possibilities. "Count it twice," she said. "Then write the number on the slip."

He counted it twice. Twenty short, both times. Laurent had already gone to the back, and the store had that after-hours hush where the coolers hum like they're rehearsing something. Cameron stood there doing what he'd been doing all night, which was assembling a version of the evening in which he was careful. He was always careful. He gave correct change. He counted back the bills. Somewhere in his chest a small voice pointed out that the voice was not evidence.

He went back to the problem instead, because the problem was cleaner. He drew the two countries again, arrows between them, and tried to see what the arrows were for. If you give up the same thing I give up, he thought, then whatever I switch to making, you're not better off getting it from me. There's nothing to trade for. It wasn't a printing error; it was the whole point. The model needed a difference, a gap you could live inside, or specialization gained you nothing. He wrote that in the margin over his earlier note, and the two notations sat there together, wrong and then less wrong, which was as close as he got to understanding anything that night.

His phone buzzed. Amelia: identical ratios means neither one has a comparative advantage. that's the answer, no trick. Then, a second later: also did you see the review sheet, question 6 is exactly this.

He was still holding the phone when the image came back to him, whole and unwelcome: the man with the paint cans, quarter to nine, in a hurry, holding out a fifty and a twenty and a ten for a forty-dollar total, and Cameron, reaching for the ten, giving him the twenty instead, both of them laughing about the paint fumes. He checked the receipt log. 8:47, forty dollars even, paid fifty, change due ten.

"Ms. Hu," he called toward the back, and his voice cracked a little on the second word. "I know where the twenty went. I gave a guy the wrong bill at nine o'clock. It's not missing, it's walking around in his wallet."

She came back out drying her hands on a towel. He slid the receipt across the counter, the margins of his homework still crowding its edges, arrows and ratios and the word comparative half-written in pencil.

"Write it on the slip," she said. "Under the number."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: For an accurate reading, a person should sit quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around Grandpa Frank's arm for the third time that afternoon, and Madeline leaned over the little screen like it might confess. One thirty-eight over eighty-six. She wrote it in her notebook, beneath two other numbers, and frowned.

"You look like a woman reading tea leaves," Grandpa said from the kitchen chair, rolling his sleeve back down.

"I look like a woman who has to pass a placement test in August, and who keeps getting different numbers from the same arm." She had been accepted into the nursing program on the condition that she complete a health assessment module over the summer, and the module's first unit, the one she'd been assigned that morning, was blood pressure: how to read it, and how diet and exercise were supposed to change it. The packet had diagrams. The diagrams had arrows. None of it explained why Grandpa's systolic number had bounced between 128 and 142 in twenty minutes.

Her phone buzzed on the counter. Carly, from the pharmacy across town: "the machine here spat out 150 over 95 for me and I nearly called a priest. thoughts?" Milana had replied to the group thread a minute later with a single acerbic "you ran here from the bus stop, genius."

Madeline typed back a question mark, and Carly sent a longer message: "I dashed in, slapped my arm in, grabbed the readout while still kind of power walking in place? then I sat in the waiting chair answering your texts for a while and tried again and it was like 126 over 82. machines are liars."

Madeline stood very still in the warm kitchen, holding the phone. Carly had rushed. Carly had then sat. The number had come down, a lot, without any pill or miracle in between. She looked at her grandfather, who had just walked in from the garage where he'd been arguing with a lawnmower, and who was sitting with one ankle crossed over his knee, bouncing it.

"Grandpa. Put both feet flat on the floor."

"I'm comfortable."

"You're comfortable like a jackhammer." She uncrossed his ankle herself, set his foot down, then slid a dictionary under the arm of the chair and propped his forearm on the stack of cushions until his elbow sat level with his heart, or close to it. "Now nobody talks. For five minutes. Not even about the lawnmower."

"Especially not about the lawnmower," Grandma called from the hallway, and Grandpa made a wounded noise and then, mercifully, went quiet.

Madeline sat across from him and let herself drift a little, into a brief reverie about August: a real uniform, a real ward, a cuff in her own two hands. Then she caught herself daydreaming on the clock and started counting the seconds on the oven timer instead. Grandpa watched her watch the timer. The refrigerator hummed. At four minutes he opened his mouth, caught her eye, and closed it again, pantomiming zipping his lips.

At five minutes she wrapped the cuff, matched his arm to the mark, and pressed start. The machine whirred, squeezed, released. One twenty-four over seventy-eight.

"That's lower," she said slowly, writing it down. "That's much lower. Same person, same machine." She looked at her earlier numbers and understood that she hadn't been measuring her grandfather at all; she'd been measuring the lawnmower, the crossed ankle, the garage walk, all of it folded into the reading like laundry shoved in a closet.

She texted the group: "Carly you accidentally did science. You have to sit still about five minutes first, feet flat, and the arm has to be supported at heart level. Posture and activity change the numbers. That's why your two readings fought." Carly replied with seventeen exclamation points. Milana sent "so I've been diagnosing my whole family mid-sprint, cool, cool."

Grandpa flexed his fingers, getting the feeling back. "So which number is my real one?"

"That's the thing." She tapped the notebook. "The second one, probably. Or, I mean, I'd want to do it a few more days in a row before I said anything definite. The module also says the numbers move for other reasons I haven't gotten to yet." She refused, on principle, to equivocate with a man who took fish-oil capsules on faith. "But the quiet one is the honest one. Today, at least."

"Today, at least," Grandpa repeated, pleased, as though she'd quoted poetry. He stood, reclaimed his sleeve, and pointed at the fridge. "Your grandmother made lemon bars. Consider it a controlled experiment: my arm, my diet, my sitting still, and one lemon bar."

"Half a lemon bar," Madeline said, already reaching for the plate. "For accuracy."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper 'The Strength of Weak Ties' found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.
story:
The party had been Judith's idea, and Amy had let herself believe for one afternoon that it was a kindness rather than a verdict. Judith's backyard was strung with vestigial Christmas lights, half of them dead, left over from some winter nobody wanted to take down. Marina had made a cake with Amy's name misspelled in blue icing. Twenty people Amy had known since third grade stood around a folding table of chips, and Amy moved among them like a guest at her own trial.

She was leaving in nine days. That part was true. What she had told them, over and over, was that she hadn't wanted to move, that her mother's transfer was a disaster imposed on them both. This was mostly a lie. Amy had found the rental listing on her mother's laptop in March and had said, quietly, "It looks nice," and her mother had taken that as permission, or at least as ammunition. So the grief she performed tonight was an amalgam of real feeling and borrowed feeling, and she could no longer separate the two, which was its own kind of honesty, she supposed.

Marina caught her by the fence. "You never told me how you got the job," she said. "The café one. You said something in the group chat and then never explained."

Amy had gotten the job in June, before she'd even seen the new town. Her neighbor there, Ms. Nolan, had mentioned a café that needed Saturday help; Amy had met her exactly twice, once at the moving inspection and once at the hardware store, and somehow that was enough. She had meant to tell Marina the whole story weeks ago. Instead she'd said it was luck, which wasn't quite a lie either.

"It's this thing," Amy said. "My cousin told me about it. Sociologist Mark Granovetter, 1973, a paper called 'The Strength of Weak Ties.' He found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends." She heard how rehearsed it sounded, like she'd been waiting at this fence for someone to ask.

Marina frowned. "Acquaintances. Like Ms. Nolan."

"Like Ms. Nolan," Amy said. "I've met her twice."

"So we're the close friends," Marina said slowly, "and the close friends are the useless ones."

"I didn't say useless."

"You didn't have to. Granovetter said it." Marina laughed, but not the way she usually laughed, and Amy felt the ground tilt slightly, the way it did when you realize a conversation has been about something else the whole time.

The twist, when it came, was not the one Amy had been bracing for. She had spent the evening expecting someone to accuse her of wanting to leave, of manufacturing her mother's opportunity with that one soft sentence in March. Instead Judith appeared at the fence with two paper cups and said, "Marina's mom called mine yesterday. About the goodbye speech. Amy, did you actually give one? Because everyone's been saying you did, at the park, last weekend, and I wasn't invited, and I'm the one who threw this." Amy had given no speech. She had not been to the park. But twenty people at this party apparently believed she had stood on a picnic table and thanked them, and some version of that Amy, the graceful one, was now more real to them than the one holding a warm cup of soda in a dead woman's Christmas lights.

"I wasn't there," Amy said.

"Then who's telling everyone you were?"

They stood in the noise of it. Somewhere behind her a boy she'd kissed once in tenth grade was playing a song from that year, and someone was singing along badly, and the whole event, she understood, was an underwriting of a story the group would keep telling after she was gone, with or without her consent. Even her denials would be folded in. Even Marina's hurt would become a detail in a version where Amy had chosen the new town, the new job, the weak ties, over all of them, and maybe that version was truer than the one Amy told herself on good days.

Marina looked at her for a long moment. "Is it a good job?" she asked.

"It's a café," Amy said. "It's Saturdays. It's probably nothing."

"But you're going to walk in there and know a person, and that person will know you, and in a year you'll have a whole life I can't see."

The lights overhead buzzed, the living half of them flickering as if deciding. Judith was still waiting by the table, watching. Amy thought of Ms. Nolan's face, half-remembered, at a hardware store three states away, and of Granovetter counting his jobs, and of the difference between an acquaintance and a friend, which she could recite and could not, tonight, feel.

"Come visit," Amy said. "Before you're an acquaintance."

Marina picked up the cake knife and cut herself the first slice, which was supposed to be Amy's, and held it out across the fence. "Say that again in a year," she said, "if you still mean it."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2011 analysis of the Dunedin Study found that children with lower self-control were more likely to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions as adults.
story:
Lucas had never once missed a shift at the school store, a fact he mentioned to anyone who stood still long enough, and usually twice to Daphnee, who worked the register next to him. He considered himself the responsible one. This was the version of events he preferred, and he saw no reason to trouble it with details, such as the Tuesday he'd traded his shift for Camilo's snack money and then simply not shown up, a memory he kept in a drawer he rarely opened.

The problem was Camilo. Camilo had skipped four shifts in three weeks, and each time the job of covering fell to Lucas, because Lucas was there and Lucas was dependable and Lucas had, he told himself, nothing better to do. On the fifth occasion, Camilo didn't even pretend. He walked past the store window with a girl from his chemistry class and waved, cheerful as a flag.

"You're doing it again," Daphnee said. She was restocking lanyards, which nobody had bought since orientation. "That face. The one where you're writing his biography."

"I'm not." He was. He was deciding that Camilo was going nowhere, and that he, Lucas, was going somewhere, although where exactly had lately become harder to enunciate. He had a college application essay due Monday, four hundred words on a challenge he'd overcome, and a draft consisting of one deleted sentence.

That night he did what he always did when avoiding writing: research. He was looking for something about habits, partly for the essay, mostly to confirm what he already believed about Camilo. He found a study instead, a long one, following a thousand people in a town called Dunedin from childhood into adulthood. An analysis of it from 2011 said that children with lower self-control were more likely, as adults, to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions. He read it twice. Then he looked at the essay document, which was still blank, and did not feel quite as sanguine about himself as he had that afternoon.

He tried out the fact on Daphnee the next day, in the supply closet where the expired granola bars lived. "There's this study," he said. "Kids with lower self-control end up with worse health, less money, criminal records. Like, actual convictions."

"So you looked up whether Camilo's doomed."

"I looked up psychology." She raised one eyebrow, which was her whole rebuttal. "Fine. Partially whether Camilo's doomed."

Daphnee, who was taking philosophy as an elective and enjoyed deploying words like "phenomenology" at people who could not stop her, said that you couldn't study a life from outside, that being observed by Lucas in a store window was not the same as being Camilo. Lucas said that was exactly the kind of thing someone with a blank essay would say, and she said it was exactly the kind of thing someone with a blank essay would hear, and they called it a draw.

The plan he came up with was simple, which should have warned him. He would tell Camilo about the study, plainly, without moralizing, and Camilo would understand that small choices compounded, and he would start showing up. Instead Camilo listened in the hallway, nodding, and then said, "Wait, so you covered my shifts to prove a point about my future?" Lucas opened his mouth to explain that this was not the sequence of events, only to discover that it was, in fact, approximately the sequence of events. He had been collecting Camilo's failures like evidence, and had let his own work quietly rot while he did it. Somewhere between the study and the hallway he understood that both things could be true at once, that Camilo was probably sailing toward exactly the outcomes the researchers described, and that Lucas's habit of watching other people's choices instead of making his own was not, on the evidence, meaningfully different in kind. He could not prove this. He was honest with himself about that much, at least.

He stayed late that night and wrote the essay, four hundred words about a challenge he was still in the middle of, and on Thursday he told Mr. Bouchard he'd take the Friday shift, his own this time, and Camilo's too, but that it was the last one, said out loud, where Camilo could hear it. Camilo showed up anyway, ten minutes late, tying his apron while the line formed.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: If people trust a central bank to keep inflation low, they ask for smaller wage and price increases, and that expectation itself helps keep inflation down.
story:
Olivier had promised his mother he would return her library books before the mall closed, which was how he came to be standing outside the electronics shop at seven o'clock on a Thursday, holding four hardbacks about gardening, while Gordon and Will argued about lemonade.

The argument was hypothetical, which was the problem. Will's uncle had once run a stand at a farmers' market, and Will had absorbed from this the conviction that any business survived by raising prices early. "If you know the cups are going to cost more next month," Will said, steering them past the perfume counter, "you raise your price now, and you're not caught out." Gordon, who had failed the same economics test Olivier had failed, said that was greed disguised as strategy, and that customers would just walk away.

"You're both assuming the customer is a stone," Olivier said. He hadn't planned to say it. The phrase had arrived from somewhere near the economics unit they'd all skimmed, the one with the diagrams he'd photographed but never read.

"A stone?"

"Someone who doesn't expect anything." He shifted the books under his arm. "If the customer thinks everything's going to cost more next month, they look at your lemonade, they believe you, and they pay the higher price without much fuss. Or they ask their boss for more money because their rent is going up, and their boss raises prices to cover it. What people expect changes what they do. It's not greed. It's weather."

Will slowed near the escalator. "So if everyone thinks prices are going up, prices go up. Because everyone's bracing for it."

"Because everyone's bracing for it," Olivier said, and felt the strange pleasure of a sentence he had not known he owned. He tried pushing further. "Which means the opposite should work too. If people believed prices were going to stay steady, they'd ask for less. Smaller raises, smaller increases. And that itself would keep things low, without anyone actually doing anything. The expectation does the work."

Gordon looked at him with the flat expression of someone watching a friend develop a new personality. "This is tangential to lemonade."

"It is the lemonade."

At the food court, Mr. Yilmaz from the history department was eating alone with a paperback, and Olivier felt the pull of an audience. Mr. Yilmaz taught a unit on the Cold War and had once used the word "problematize" in a sentence about homework, which half the class had resented. Olivier did not go over. He was seventeen and had learned that explaining a thing you half-understood in front of a teacher was a way of volunteering to fail publicly. Instead they took the table beside him, and Olivier laid out his thinking anyway, more quietly, because he could not stop.

"So imagine the lemonade stand has a manager," he said. "And everyone in the neighbourhood trusts the manager to keep prices reasonable. Genuinely trusts it, the way you trust a bridge. Then when the stand hints at a price hike, nobody panics. Nobody braces. People ask for smaller increases, the stand asks for smaller increases, and it stays low. The trust itself is doing half the managing."

"Where'd you read that?" Gordon said.

"Nowhere. Probably somewhere. Maybe I got it wrong." He turned his cup on the table. "The part I can't tell is whether the trust comes from the manager being trustworthy or from everyone deciding to trust the manager. Those seem like different things, and the diagram in the textbook only had one arrow." This admission sat in the middle of the table for a while. Will ate his fries. Gordon looked at the fountain two levels down, where coins lay in the water like a broken scoreboard.

Mr. Yilmaz turned a page without looking up and said, to his book, "There's a reason the reading was optional and the test wasn't."

Olivier put his mother's books on the chair beside him, squared them, and watched a toddler throw a coin into the fountain, the small splash swallowed immediately by the water.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Many ethicists distinguish doing harm from allowing harm, and most people judge causing a harm as worse than failing to prevent an equal harm, though some philosophers reject the distinction.
story:
Ms. Delgado had a habit of rapping her knuckles twice on the whiteboard whenever she wanted a word to stick, and that morning the word was "consequences." Henry copied it down without thinking, because his mind was still on Saturday, on the dark ring of dead grass spreading across Mr. Okafor's lawn, and on the fact that he had said nothing about it for two days.

The class was arguing about a runaway trolley, the famous case Willy had looked up the night before and now recited with the smugness of a boy who believed research was the same as being right. Five people on the straight track, one on the spur, a lever in your hand. Willy said you pull the lever; the arithmetic was obvious. Eli, peevish that morning because his bus had been late and his coffee cold, said the arithmetic was exactly what was wrong with it. "You're not just letting five die," he said. "You're steering the thing. There's a difference between doing and watching."

"Actually," Willy said, and Henry knew what was coming, because Willy began most of his sentences that way, a mannerism Ms. Delgado had once gently parodied at a class party, "some philosophers reject the distinction entirely."

Ms. Delgado rapped the board twice. "That's the word," she said. "Distinction. Most ethicists separate doing harm from allowing harm, and most people judge causing a harm as worse than failing to prevent an equal one. But not everyone accepts that." Then she stepped back and let the room fight, which was her way.

Henry looked at the lever drawn in dry-erase marker, a simple line on a simple track, and thought about the fertilizer spreader. His father had told him to use the setting for the front lawn. Henry had misread the dial, or hadn't read it, and the concentrated mix had spilled along the property line. He had hosed it down, raked the crust into the soil, and told himself it would be fine. Then the rain came, and the runoff went where runoff goes, and by Monday morning the neighbor's lawn had a brown crescent near the shared border, widening like a stain on a shirt.

Here was the part he kept circling. He hadn't poisoned Mr. Okafor's grass on purpose. He had caused it, though, plainly caused it, with his own hands and a dial he could have checked. And then, knowing, he had walked past the window each morning and said nothing. If the distinction mattered, which act was his? The spilling, or the silence? His mother, at dinner on Sunday, had put down her fork and said that not telling was its own decision, that a lie of omission was still a lie, and his father had said, "It's not the same thing, and you know it. An accident isn't an ambush." They had gone back and forth over the lasagna while Henry pushed his food around, and he still couldn't decide which of them he agreed with, or whether he was just hoping one of them would decide for him.

Around him the class had moved from trolleys to a drowning child in a pond, shoes getting ruined, distance getting invoked. Eli argued that if you'd denigrate the man who won't ruin his shoes, you ought to treat the person who does the harm even more harshly, and Willy argued that the outcomes were identical and identical outcomes deserved identical judgments. Ms. Delgado wrote both claims on the board and underlined neither. Henry found himself, for the first time all class, raising his hand.

"Say the lever thing is real," he said, when she nodded at him. "Say you caused something, small, a while ago. And then afterward you didn't fix it, and you knew you weren't fixing it. Are those two separate things you did, or one thing stretched out over time?"

Eli turned in his seat. "What did you do?"

"That's the thing," Henry said. "The hypothetical never says."
