Ms. Delgado did not press him, though he caught the small shift in her expression, the way she set the marker down and gave him a moment to continue instead of moving on. He didn't continue. The bell rang, and the class broke into the noise of chairs and zippers, and Willy clap ped him on the shoulder on the way out and said, "Bro, your hypotheticals are weirdly specific."

Henry was the last one out, which meant he was the one who heard Ms. Delgado say, not unkindly, to his back: "Hypotheticals usually are."

He took the long way home, past the hardware store, and stood for a while in front of the seed display before he bought a bag of patch grass and a receipt he folded into his pocket. At the Okafor fence he stopped, looked at the brown crescent, then at his own shoes, then at their doorbell, and stood there with his hand half raised, ringing nothing yet.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: Mozart's works are identified by K numbers from the catalogue compiled by Ludwig von Köchel, first published in 1862.
story:
The fan in Bryanna's window clicked through its rotations like a metronome nobody had asked for, and the July air it moved around did nothing so much as enervate Adam, who sat cross-legged on her living room rug with the score of a Mozart piano sonata open in front of him. He was supposed to be learning to hear the shape of the thing, to mark where the exposition ended and the development began, to catch the moment the recapitulation gathered all those wandering keys and carried them home. By Monday he had to do it cold, in a placement exam that decided whether he got into the conservatory's theory stream in the fall, and so far the movement lay on the page like a city seen from a plane, all lights and no streets.

"Start with the first theme," Bryanna said, chewing the end of a pencil. She had taken the exam last year and passed it, a fact she never mentioned and never quite stopped radiating. "Find where it settles. That's your exposition."

"That's what the book says." He played the opening bars from memory on the air with his fingers. "But the second theme doesn't feel like a different thing to me. It feels like the same thing wearing a different coat. If I mark it wrong I lose the whole structure."

Bryanna's older brother came through in a hedonistic sprawl of towel and wet sandals, fresh from the pool, and dropped a folded programme on the coffee table before collapsing onto the couch. "Concert tonight," he said to the ceiling. "Free tickets from work. Some pianist. There's a Mozart on it, actually." He picked up Adam's score, glanced at it, and laughed. "K. 331. Hey, that's the one in my programme. Same number. Weird coincidence."

Adam's stomach did something quiet and complicated. He had chosen the piece at random from the anthology three weeks ago. Now it was going to be played, live, four streets away, in ninety minutes, and he had not yet managed to hear its form, only to read about it.

"What's the K. even stand for?" Bryanna asked her brother.

"No idea. It's just printed after the title. Everybody nods like they know."

The withheld thing, the thing Adam had told nobody, was that he had already sat this exam once in the spring and failed the analysis section by two marks. His parents thought he was going to a study session. He was, technically. He had not said he would be sitting in a concert hall tonight with the answers walking past him, either.

They walked over together, the three of them, the streetlights coming on in that slow way that makes a whole neighbourhood seem to hold its breath. In the lobby Adam studied the programme under a sconce. After the title, sure enough, the letters sat there in small italics, K. 331, as though everyone were born knowing what they meant. He turned the programme over, then its inside pages, and found nothing but advertisements for a piano showroom.

The hall doors were still closed, so he climbed to the mezzanine where the record shop used to be before it became a shelf of donated sleeves in the theatre's lobby. Mr. Littlechild, who lived two doors from Bryanna and volunteered here on Fridays, was sorting the donations. Adam had avoided him since the spring, since the exam, since the afternoon Mr. Littlechild had asked how it had gone and Adam had said fine.

"You looking for something specific or hiding?" Mr. Littlechild asked, not unkindly, and Adam, after a moment, held up the programme and pointed at the letters.

Mr. Littlechild didn't launch into anything. He just pulled a battered LP from the sorting crate and handed it over. The back of the sleeve had a note, dense and old, and Adam read it standing under the dim light while the lobby emptied and the first bell rang. Mozart's works were identified by K numbers from the catalogue compiled by Ludwig von Köchel, first published in 1862. That was all. A botanist of a man, Adam thought, pressing flowers that had already dried, and yet without him every sonata would be floating loose, nameless, dateless, a city with no street signs.

"Köchel," Adam said to Bryanna as they found their seats, whispering it fast before the lights dimmed. "The numbers are from his catalogue. 1862."

"Where'd you learn that?"

"Read it." The pianist came out, bowed, sat.

The movement began, the same opening Adam had played on the air all afternoon, but live it moved differently, slower, and he stopped trying to mark sections in his head and just listened. When the development came he felt it before he could name it, a tilting, a shadow crossing the tune, and he understood suddenly that the form wasn't a diagram but an argument, a dialectic of statement and departure, and that the recapitulation would be the same theme changed by everything it had been through. The question that stayed open, that he would carry into Monday, was whether the second theme was truly new or the first transformed, and he suspected now that the honest answer was that the distinction was a tool, not a truth.

The final chords settled, the hall held its silence, and Adam sat with his eyes closed.

"Did you mark it?" Bryanna whispered.

"I think I did," he said, and kept his eyes closed for one more bar.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the second derivative test, if f'(a) = 0 and f''(a) is negative, the function has a local maximum at x = a.
story:
The kitchen table still smelled of the onions his father had chopped an hour earlier, and Edouard had spread his graph paper over the damp ring the pot had left, because the table was the only surface in the apartment big enough for both his notebook and the biology reading he was supposed to finish by Monday. The retake was Tuesday morning. Ms. Morales had said it plainly, without cruelty, holding his first exam out to him like a receipt: a 41, and the derivative problems marked with red hooks that looked almost like check marks until you looked twice. He had until Tuesday to learn what he had spent a semester pretending to learn.

His phone lay face down beside the salt. Allen had texted four times since dinner, the last message a photo of Raymond's car packed with coolers, and Edouard knew that if he turned the phone over he would find a fifth. He did not turn it over. Instead he copied the problem from the board photos he had taken, the ones he'd taken to look diligent rather than to study: f(x) equals negative x cubed plus twelve x minus five, if he was reading his own handwriting correctly, and underneath it Ms. Morales's instruction, find the maximum.

He had gotten that far on the first exam and then stalled. Differentiating was not the problem; the power rule had a pleasing bluntness, drop the exponent down, subtract one, and he could do it while half-asleep. So f prime was negative three x squared plus twelve, and he set it equal to zero and solved, and got x equals two and x equals negative two. Two critical points. And then, on the exam, he had written "maximum at x equals 2" because 2 was positive and positive meant up, which even at the time he had suspected was not mathematics but superstition.

Now he sat with his pencil circling the number 2 and could not tell, looking at it, whether the curve rose to it or fell through it. A critical point could be either, he understood that much; the curve could touch zero slope at a peak or at the bottom of a valley, and the flatness at the top of a hill was identical to the flatness at the bottom of a ditch. He was trying to picture the whole graph in his head and the picture kept collapsing. His father came through for water, stood behind him a moment, said nothing, and went back to the television, where a nature program murmured about a river that had divided a population of fish until the two halves became, over ten thousand years, separate species, a process the narrator called speciation. One river, two fish that could no longer recognize each other. Edouard wrote speciation in the margin of his biology notes and underlined it twice, then felt the small dishonesty of underlining a word he would not read about tonight.

He almost picked up the phone then. Not for the party, exactly, but because Allen had a way of cutting through these dead ends, and because sitting alone with a stubborn problem had begun to enervate him, that specific tiredness that was not sleepiness but a draining of the will to continue. He reached for the phone and stopped with his hand on it. Allen would give him the answer. Allen would say which x it was, and Edouard would write it down, and Tuesday morning he would face a slightly different problem with the same hole in his understanding, and the hole would go on swallowing things quietly for the rest of his life, the way his uncle's had, the way his father's had, a family of men who could follow steps but not tell a hill from a valley.

He turned back to the page. There had to be a way to know. He sketched the two points, guessing at the curve's shape, and the guesses contradicted each other; if the function went up to x equals 2, then what was happening at x equals negative 2? He differentiated again, because he could, because it was the one move he had. Negative six x. Then f double prime of two was negative twelve. He looked at that minus sign for a long moment. The slope of the slope was negative, which meant, if he was reading it right, that the first derivative was itself decreasing through that point, climbing and then tipping over into descent, like a hiker reaching a crest. He checked x equals negative two: positive twelve. A valley. "It's a local maximum," he said out loud to the empty kitchen, testing the words, and his father glanced over from the couch. "At x equals 2."

He verified it the crude way, plugging in values on either side of 2, and the outputs rose and then fell, and there it was, a peak he had found not by guessing the picture but by pressing on the function until it told him its own shape. Something loosened in his chest. He would have liked to call Allen and say he'd gotten it, and he picked up the phone with that intention, but what he found instead was the fifth photo, the whole group at the lake in the last orange light, Raymond holding up a soda like a trophy, and beneath it a single question mark. He typed, then deleted it, then set the phone back beside the salt, screen down, and started the next problem, pencil moving through the second derivative while the fish drifted apart on the muted television behind him.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
story:
Annabelle arrived at the community art studio forty minutes before it closed, a poster tube under one arm and a coil of copper wire in her jacket pocket. The flyer on the studio door had promised a public printer, a laminator, and someone at the desk who could sell her cardstock, and so far all three promises had held. Mr. Becker, the man at the desk, slid a laminating pouch across the counter without looking up from his crossword.

"It has to be printed bigger," she said. "A3. I designed it on A4."

"Printer's behind you. Two dollars a sheet."

The design was for the spring showcase at the library: a copper-wire tree pressed flat against the page, its branches traced in pencil and then wrapped, glued, photographed, and reduced to a print she could afford to copy sixty times. She had spent three weekends on the wire alone, heating it with a borrowed torch until the metal went ductile enough to bend into the small crooked fingers of the lower branches. Now the whole thing had to live on paper.

She fed the file to the printer and asked it for A3. The machine hummed, pulled, paused, and delivered a sheet twice the size of her original, and the tree sat in the corner of it, unchanged, stubbornly small. She had told the printer to scale and it had not, or she had told it wrong, or the file had a lock on its dimensions. Whatever the cause, the page came out nearly blank.

Kellyann came in with paint under her fingernails, heading for the back room where the life-drawing group met on Thursdays. She stopped at the printer long enough to laugh. "You dichotomize everything," she said. "Either the machine is broken or you are. Try telling it fit to page."

Annabelle tried fit to page. This time the tree filled the A3 sheet exactly, edge to edge, every crooked finger of wire arriving in its place, and nothing had been cropped. She held the A3 print next to her original A4 and the two versions matched. Not almost. Exactly.

Last spring, before any of this, she had sat in the library's copy room with Blake, trying to enlarge a zine page for a protest banner. They had guessed at percentages, printed eleven wrong copies, and Blake had finally slapped the money down for a large-format shop that got it wrong a different way. She remembered him peeling the ruined banner off the table, saying the whole thing was rigged, that nothing scaled cleanly and you just paid until it looked close enough. She had believed him for a year.

She set the two sheets side by side on the counter. "The A3 is double the A4," she said slowly, "and it's the same shape. It didn't stretch anything."

Mr. Becker laid down his pen. In the studio's back room, someone dropped a jar of brushes, and Kellyann swore with feeling. The sound carried, and Blake came out of the back room with the life-drawing group's coffee order in his hands, because he had apparently joined the life-drawing group at some point in the winter without telling her, and he stood there holding four cups and looking at her poster.

"That's the copper thing," he said.

"It prints clean at A3. It doubles and the shape holds."

"No way." He put the coffees down on the counter, which Mr. Becker allowed for reasons he did not state. Blake took the A4 sheet, folded it in half the short way, and tore it, and held the two halves up beside the A3 print. The halves matched the big sheet's proportions. He looked at the torn paper for a long second. "The sides are one to the square root of two," he said. "That's why. Cut it in half and you get two of the same shape. It's the ISO thing, A4, A3, all of them."

"So the banner wasn't rigged," Annabelle said. "We just didn't know."

"We could have known." He said it flatly, and she understood that some of his anger that spring had never been about the printer. He had been the one who wanted the banner perfect, and she had been the one who said close enough was fine, and each of them had spent a year thinking the other had given up first.

She took the torn halves back from him. Mr. Becker slid another laminating pouch toward her without comment, and the printer behind her was already warm, and the showcase wanted sixty copies by Saturday, which meant tonight she had to decide whether to print the run at A4 and trust the smaller size, or pay for A3 and carry tubes home on the bus. The copper tree in her pocket, the original, the real one, was small enough to close her hand around. She fed the A3 file back into the queue and listened to the machine begin to pull.

Kellyann called from the back room that the model was early and someone had to move the easels, and Blake picked up three of the coffees and left one on the counter next to her, still steaming.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: The AP 2-D Art and Design portfolio's Selected Works section asks for 5 artworks and counts for 40 percent of the score.
story:
Luca spread eleven photographs across the worktable at the community art studio, weighting the curling corners with pencils and jar lids because he had run out of everything else. The afternoon light came through the tall windows in wide bars, and dust moved through it so slowly that he could follow a single mote from the shelf of glazes to the floor. For six weeks he had been making pictures of doors: doors boarded over, doors ajar, a screen door with a hole the shape of a fist, his grandmother's front door the winter before she moved. The assignment was a sustained investigation, ten works around one idea, and an artist's statement explaining what the work was about. He had the ten. The trouble was the other part.

He had heard it from Romane, who had read the college board's pages more carefully than anyone, and he had checked it himself twice. The Selected Works section asked for five artworks and counted for forty percent of the score. Five pieces. Forty percent. He kept repeating it to himself the way you repeat a combination lock, and the rest, the whole sustained investigation he had built his semester around, was worth less than half. Which meant that half of his future depended on choosing his five strongest works, and he could not tell which five those were, because the ones he loved were not always the ones that were good.

Veronica arrived at four with her portfolio under one arm and a paper cup of tea she never finished. She looked at the spread on the table and pulled a stool over without asking. "You've got eleven down," she said. "Bold."

"I have too many," Luca said. "I need five and I can't get below six without feeling like I'm lying."

"About what?"

"About which ones matter." He touched the edge of the photograph of the screen door. "This one's the truest. It's also the weakest, technically. The focus is soft at the top." He touched a second picture, a row of steel doors in a hospital corridor, perfectly sharp, perfectly cold. "This one's the best made. And it might be the least mine."

Veronica drank her tea and looked for a long time. She had a way of looking that was not generous or stingy but judicious, weighing each image the way Ms. Ramos had taught them to weigh glaze tests, noting what fired true and what ran. "You keep saying truest like it's a measurement," she said. "It's not. But soft focus at the top of a door is a choice if you say it's a choice."

Ms. Ramos came out of the kiln room with clay dust on her forearms and stood behind them. She did not offer an opinion, which Luca had learned was her version of respect. Instead she asked him to say his theme out loud. He said doors, and she shook her head and waited, and he said barriers, and she shook her head again, and finally he said that it was about what a threshold feels like from inside, the moment before you decide whether to go through. She nodded once and went back to the kiln room, and Veronica raised an eyebrow at him.

He had been thinking, all semester, that the two halves of the portfolio were competing: the honest pictures against the skilled ones, the investigation against the selection, as if he had to proselytize for one or the other. His father, who worked in insurance, talked about art the way he talked about anything, as a thing you either had a knack for or didn't, a fixed quantity. His photography teacher freshman year had talked about it the opposite way, as pure craft, all decisions and no soul, and Luca had absorbed both voices without noticing they argued. Sitting in the barred light, he began to suspect they were both wrong, or rather that each was describing only half of a thing that didn't split cleanly. The softness at the top of the screen door could be an apology or could be an intention, and the difference was not in the photograph. The difference was in what he claimed for it, and whether he could stand behind the claim.

He pulled the steel corridor picture aside, then pulled it back. He laid out six in a row and made himself imagine the stranger who would open his portfolio in some office in May, a person who did not know his grandmother, did not know the hospital, did not know him at all. The thought frightened him and then, oddly, steadied him. If the whole thing was solipsism, pictures only he could read, then no five would save it. If it wasn't, then the stranger would meet him halfway, and his job was to leave the door open for that meeting.

He chose the screen door. He chose the hospital corridor too, and three others, and when Veronica asked him why those, he said, "Because I can defend every one of them out loud." It was the first sentence all afternoon he had said without hesitating.

He still had the artist's statement to write, and the honest worry that he had chosen one true picture over a better one, or the reverse, and no way to know until the scores came. Veronica gathered her portfolio and left her tea on the table, a small amber ring forming under the cup. Luca began sliding his photographs back into the case, one at a time, the screen door last.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
Levi had bowled exactly once before tonight, which was one more time than he let on, and he'd spent the afternoon rehearsing the parts of himself he planned to show. He arrived at Sunset Lanes nine minutes early, which he intended Alexandria to interpret as reliability rather than anxiety, and he watched the parking lot through the pro shop window while the smell of rental shoes and blue sanitizing powder settled into his jacket. When she pulled in, in her brother's dented Civic, he raised a hand that he hoped looked casual and thought it probably looked like a man hailing a bus.

"You said eight, right?" Alexandria said, coming through the glass doors with her own shoes in a bag, which he took as a good sign, a sign of seriousness, a sign that she had done this before, though he did not ask with whom. He said eight was right, and that he came early because traffic had been light, which was true, and also because he'd been sitting in his room since six unable to read the same page of a magazine, which he left out.

They got lane fourteen. Ace worked the shoe counter, having somehow gotten a job there in October, and he grinned at Levi with a denigrating slowness, the grin of someone who'd watched Levi gutter three consecutive balls at a birthday party in eighth grade and had never let the memory die. "Lucky lane," Ace said. "For some people." Levi laughed as though it didn't matter, and selected a twelve-pound ball because Alexandria selected a twelve-pound ball, and he understood that he was being a mirror, and he did it anyway.

He threw his first ball into the gutter. He had a story ready about his wrist, an old skateboarding injury that had never actually prevented him from doing anything, but Alexandria was already saying "same," because her ball had gone into the other gutter, and her laugh was so easy that he felt the falseness in his pocket like a stone he could put down. She asked him what he was actually good at, and he said, honestly, that he wasn't sure yet, and she said that was the first non-boring thing anyone had said to her all week.

The score screen kept flashing an ad for the midnight haunted maze in the back lot, sponsored by the arcade, $10, ENTER IF YOU DARE. Alexandria leaned toward it. "I love those," she said. "The bad ones. Where the guy in the hockey mask jumps out at you and you can hear the zipper on his costume." Levi said he loved them too, and in his memory this was almost true; there had been one, two years ago, with Ms. Chen's son, where he had screamed in a register he'd been grateful no one recorded. The narrator he kept in his head insisted he was hard to frighten. His body had a different record, and a longer one.

Between frames he told her about a study he'd found at two in the morning, weeks ago, when he'd been looking up why his chest felt the way it did whenever she turned around in chemistry before he'd even said a word to her. "In 1974," he said, "these two researchers, Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, had a woman interview men on a scary suspension bridge, the kind that sways, the kind your body treats like a mistake. And the men who'd just crossed the frightening bridge were more likely to call her afterward than the men who crossed a sturdy one." He watched her line up her approach as he said it, the way she bent her knees and let the ball go with surprising, clean force.

"Call her," Alexandria repeated, straightening up. "Like, on the phone. Ask her out."

"Ask her out. That's the whole finding." He kept his voice light, though his pulse was not light, and he was aware of the irony, aware that he was standing on his own swaying bridge right now saying so. "So the question is," he said, "if we do the maze, and some guy with a chainsaw that's actually a leaf blower makes my heart pound, how would either of us know what the pounding means?"

She considered this with what he thought was real probity, no smirk, no deflection, turning the question over the way she'd turned the ball in her hands. "So you're saying the maze is cheating," she said. "Like if we go in there, we can't trust anything we feel coming out."

He had been saying something narrower, and possibly something sneakier, a nascent scheme of engineering his own attractiveness via leaf blower, and her honesty made him feel caught. He thought about arguing that maybe nothing was pure, that every date was a suspension bridge of one kind or another, the scary movie, the roller coaster, the tall ledge people took pictures from. But he also thought: if she likes me only when her heart is slamming, what do I have on an ordinary Tuesday?

"I'm saying I don't want a receipt," he said. "I'd rather find out at normal speed." It came out more serious than he'd meant, and he bowled his next ball to cover it, and the ball actually struck the pocket, pins exploding sideways, a strike, his first ever, and Ace's voice came over the intercom saying "Beginner's luck, sunset boy," and Alexandria was laughing so hard she had to sit down on the ball return.

They bowled two more frames, badly, both of them, happily. She beat him by eleven points and demanded he admit it, and he admitted it, and then she stood and held out her hand toward the back lot, toward the EXIT sign glowing over the black plastic flaps of the maze entrance, and said, "Come on. Leaf blower and all. We'll figure out which kind of pounding it is the honest way."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Kazuo Ishiguro's 1989 novel The Remains of the Day, the butler Stevens reports events accurately but misreads their meaning, including his own feelings.
story:
Mr. Mehta set the battered copies of The Remains of the Day on the desk and said the essays were due Friday, and Gabriel felt the familiar tightening in his chest, because he had read every page and understood none of it. Or not none of it. The words were clear. The butler Stevens described his days at Darlington Hall with a precision that reminded Gabriel of a mechanic listing parts. What Gabriel could not find was the thing he was supposed to be finding, the argument, the thesis, the handle on the door.

"Gabriel, you're quiet," Mr. Mehta said. "What do you make of Stevens?"

"He's reliable," Gabriel said. "He tells you exactly what happened. What time the car arrived, what the guests said."

Clementine, two seats over, made a small sound through her nose. "You can't actually believe that."

"He doesn't lie."

"Fine." She flipped her book open to a page she had already flagged, which annoyed him, the preparedness of it. "Day two, evening. He's telling you about Miss Kenton leaving the hall, and he says he wasn't upset, and then he describes standing in the corridor for a long time not moving. Read what he does and then read what he says he felt."

Gabriel read. The corridor. The stillness. Stevens reporting his own body like weather. Something shifted at the edge of his thinking and would not come into focus.

"So his facts are right and his feelings are wrong," Maira said from the window row. She said it the way she said most things, lightly, as if the answer were obvious and she was handing it over out of politeness. "He reports events accurately but misreads what they mean. Including his own."

"That's too simple," Gabriel said, though he wasn't sure it was, and the uncertainty made him say it louder than he meant. "You can't split a person into facts and feelings like that. The facts are his. He chose which ones to write down."

Mr. Mehta was writing something on the board, a single word, unreliable, and then he underlined it twice and did not turn around. "Keep going," he said. "This is the essay."

"He published it in 1989," Clementine said. "Ishiguro. It's on the cover, Gabriel."

"I know when it was published." He did know. He had stared at the copyright page the night before for reasons he could not have explained, feeling that the date mattered, that a book about a man looking back over decades was itself a decision someone made in a particular year. What he had not done was connect that to anything. He was good at collecting and bad at connecting, his mother said so, the coach said so, and now apparently Clementine was going to say so.

Maira got up and came to his desk, which she did when an argument interested her, and Gabriel felt the room sharpen. "Okay. Interpolate," she said. "You know the word? Fill in the gap. Stevens gives you the accurate event, and then between the lines you fill in what he actually felt. The book makes you do the work he can't."

"That's the trick," Clementine said, less voluble now, leaning forward instead of talking over him, which somehow felt more serious. "The point of view. You trust him because he's precise, and then the precision betrays him."

Gabriel looked down at the page again. The corridor. The butler who had given the whole of himself to a house and a man and could not say so, who used the word dignity the way other people used a coat rack, hanging gravitas on it and calling the arrangement a life. He thought about the way he had told his father the move to his mother's place was fine, and how he had said it in a level voice with his hands flat on the table, as though the hands were evidence.

"Here's what I think," Gabriel said slowly. "You're both right, and you're both missing it. He's not reliable or unreliable. He's accurate about events and wrong about meaning, at the same time, and you can't separate them because the wrongness is made out of the accuracy. That's why it works. That's why we keep reading him." He stopped. "I still don't know what I'll write for the thesis. Something like that. Half of that."

Mr. Mehta turned around at last. "Write the half you're sure of," he said. "Leave the rest honest."

At the door after the bell, Clementine caught his sleeve. "Corridor scene, day two," she said. "Start there."

He nodded and put the book in his bag, open to the page, his thumb holding the place.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The envelope was thin, and Kevin had read somewhere that thin meant no, though he could not remember where, and suspected the saying had been invented by people who needed somewhere to put their dread. He set it on the kitchen table beside his laptop, unopened, and went to the counter to refill his coffee even though the mug was still two thirds full.

His mother worked the second shift that week, so the kitchen was his until ten. On the screen was his college list, fourteen schools reduced over the autumn to nine, then to six, and now to a question he could not make the spreadsheet answer: which of them wanted him, and which of them wanted his money. His father's disability payments covered rent and not much else. Kevin had learned to read the family budget the way other kids read weather, squinting at it for signs of what was coming.

Micah arrived first, letting himself in through the back door with the ease of someone who had eaten at this table a hundred times. He carried a printout of his own list, folded into quarters, and a bag of clementines he set down without comment. Jada came ten minutes later, hair still wet from practice, and took the chair nearest the radiator, which she claimed every time as though the chair were assigned.

"Did you open it?" she asked.

"No."

"It's from State. They take everybody from our county."

"They don't take everybody."

"Practically everybody." She peeled a clementine and offered him half without looking at him, which was her way of saying she was nervous too.

Micah unfolded his printout and smoothed it with the heel of his hand. "Okay, so I need you both to look at something, because I've been going in circles." He turned the paper around. He had divided his schools into two columns, and above the left column he had written, in his careless but legible hand, the words NEED-BLIND, and above the right, NEED-AWARE. "Counselor gave me the terms on Tuesday. Need-blind admission means they decide whether to admit you without looking at whether you can pay. That's the whole thing. The other ones, most of them actually, are need-aware. They look."

Kevin pulled the printout closer. "So the right column schools are deciding, right now, whether admitting you costs them something."

"Basically, yeah."

Jada leaned over. "That's not a secret, though. It's on their websites."

"It's on a page nobody reads," Micah said. "It's on the page after the bombastic one about diversity and access, where they stop performing and start budgeting."

Kevin turned back to his own laptop and opened the financial aid page of the school at the top of his list, the small liberal arts college two states away that he had visited once, in the rain, and loved with an intensity he had not confessed to anyone. He found the page. He read it twice. Then he read it aloud, quietly, because saying it seemed to transmute it from print into something with weight. His school was need-aware.

"Yours too?" Micah asked.

Kevin nodded. He sat back. The radiator ticked. Outside, the neighbor's dog was barking at the mail truck, which was the closest thing to a deadline either of them had until May 1, the national reply date, three weeks away, by which every admitted student in the country had to choose.

"Here's what I keep thinking," Jada said. She had finished her clementine and was arranging the peels in a small star, an old habit. "You're mad at the school for looking at money. But my uncle works in admissions at a public university, and he says the need-blind places are mostly the ones with giant endowments. They can afford not to look. It's not that they're better people. They're a different stratum. They have the luxury of pretending money doesn't exist."

"I'm not mad," Kevin said, and heard how unconvincing it sounded. He pulled the thin envelope toward him and slit it with a butter knife. It was one page. State University had admitted him, and enclosed a scholarship figure that covered tuition but not housing, which was the deal they gave to practically everybody from his county, and which his mother would call a gift and he would call a beginning.

"So that's your floor," Micah said. "You have a floor now. Everything else is upside."

"That's one way to hold it."

"What's the other way?"

Kevin thought about the question honestly, because Micah deserved that. "The other way is that the need-aware schools might not take me, and I'll never know whether it was my essay or my parents' tax return. I can't make those two things separate. Nobody can." He looked at the printout, at the two columns, at the tidy way the schools had been sorted. "So maybe the right question isn't which system is fairer. Maybe it's just: which schools, given what they actually do, still make sense for me to want."

Jada pointed at the liberal arts college on his screen. "Are you withdrawing your application?"

"No. I want to see. If they take me with the aid I need, then the label didn't decide it, at least not this time. If they don't, I'll take State and the floor and be glad of both." He paused. "I'm not going to pretend I'll know why, either way. That part stays uncertain. I'm just deciding not to let the uncertainty be the whole story."

Mr. Almeida, their history teacher, lived three houses down, and Kevin had promised to return his copy of a book about the transcontinental railroad by Friday. He found the book where he had left it, on the shelf by the microwave, and slid it into his backpack. At the door, with his coat half on, he stopped and looked back at the table: Jada's star of peels, Micah's two columns, his own open laptop still glowing with the aid page, and the single sheet from State lying flat on the wood like a small white floor to stand on.

"Lock the back door when you leave," he said.

"Already done," Micah said, and turned the printout over to its blank side, as if starting fresh.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, such as a monarch or ceremonial president, from the head of government, while in the United States the president is both.
story:
Kyle carried two coffees down the empty hallway before first bell, one for himself and one for Mr. Santos, because the polling tables were being set up in the gym and Mr. Santos had the key. It was a small attempt to propitiate a man who had already said yes, but Kyle had learned from his mother that favors were best renewed before they expired. The student council election was that afternoon, and the council's own account was three dollars from insolvency after the poster debacle, so the ballots had been photocopied on the library machine at a discount Kaia had negotiated by promising to reshelve the biography section for a month.

The gym smelled of floor wax and old pep rallies. Mr. Santos took the coffee without ceremony, unlocked the folding tables, and left Kyle and Kaia to arrange them near the bleachers. Kaia lined up the pencils in a row so straight it looked like a display case. "My dad's from Norway," she said, apropos of nothing Kyle could see. "He keeps saying we vote wrong. He says a whole country can't be run like this."

"Like what?"

"Like everything hangs on one person." She squared another pencil. "He says I should ask you, because you did that project."

The project had been Kyle's and Andres's, a comparative politics presentation that had consumed most of October. Kyle remembered the night it came together: they were in Andres's kitchen, flashcards spread across the counter like a dealt hand, and Andres had finally lost patience with Kyle's summaries. "Stop listing," Andres had said. "Ask me something." Kyle had asked why the British cards kept showing the queen at state dinners while a different man answered questions in Parliament, and Andres had shrugged and said, "Because they split the jobs." That had been the hinge. From there the cards stopped being trivia and became two different logics: in a parliamentary system, the legislature chose the head of government and could unmake that person with a vote the chamber itself controlled, while a presidential system elected its chief separately, and removal was a rarer, harder ritual reserved for wrongdoing. Kyle had sat in that kitchen until nearly midnight, shuffling the two decks against each other, feeling for the first time that a constitution was not a document but a set of bets about where power should get stuck.

Now, at the polling station, a freshman stopped in front of the ballot box with his pencil hovering. "Why does Norway have a king and a prime minister?" he asked. "That's two guys. Isn't that confusing?"

Kyle glanced at Kaia, who folded her arms and gestured at him, evidently her father's proxy. "A lot of parliamentary systems separate them," Kyle said. "The monarch is the head of state, the ceremonial one, and the prime minister is the head of government, the one who actually runs things. In the United States the president is both."

"So who's the real guy?"

"Depends what you mean by real." Kyle heard his own voice get careful. "In Norway, both. The king cuts ribbons; the prime minister answers to Parliament. Here, one person does both jobs, and Congress can't just vote that person out because it's tired of them."

The freshman looked at the ballot, which offered three candidates for council president with full executive powers and no mechanism whatever for removing any of them. "So if we elect Marcus and he's terrible?"

"Then we wait," Kaia said, "for the next election."

"Or," said Andres, arriving with the absentee folder, "we could change the system. That was the whole point of your project, wasn't it? You talked about it for weeks."

Kyle had, in fact, drafted something during those weeks and then buried it in his backpack: a proposal that the council's president be chosen by and from the elected representatives, with the power to be recalled by a two-thirds vote of the council itself, and a separate, mostly ceremonial student "chair of state" to hand out awards and open the talent show. He had never shown it to anyone because it felt both too small, a constitution for an organization with a treasury of three dollars, and too large, a thing that assumed people wanted their politics rearranged.

The afternoon polls opened and the interminable procession of voters began, each one asking some version of the freshman's question, and Kyle answered each one and felt the answers sharpen under repetition. At the last bell, the three of them counted ballots on the folded tables while Mr. Santos stacked chairs in the background. Kyle took the folded proposal from his backpack and set it on the table between the ballot stacks and Kaia's row of pencils.

"So," he said. "Before we announce a winner. Do we count these, or do we talk first?"

Andres looked at the paper, then at the tally sheet, then at Kyle. Kaia picked up the proposal and began to read.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: London lies at about 51.5 degrees north, farther north than any point in the contiguous United States.
story:
Cole had promised Ms. Holloway he would be first through the museum doors, and he was, though only because he had run the last two blocks with his backpack thumping against his spine. The ocean hall opened at nine. At ten, the three of them had to stand in front of the giant current map and explain, to whoever stopped to listen, how the Gulf Stream kept northern Europe warm. Ms. Holloway called it a demonstration. Cole called it, privately, a trap, because he still could not read the map.

"Okay," Lara said, spreading her notes on the floor beneath the looping ribbons of red and blue. "Warm currents are red, cold are blue, and the arrows show direction. That part's easy."

"If it's easy, why does it look like a plate of spaghetti," Levi said. He crouched and traced a red ribbon with one finger, from the Gulf of Mexico, up along the American coast, then bending east across the Atlantic toward Europe. Cole watched the finger go and felt something loosen, slightly. The line was not spaghetti. It was a road.

"Wait," Levi said. He pulled out his phone and opened a map. "Where's London, actually? I've been saying it's like New York."

Lara leaned over. "It's way higher. Look."

Cole looked. He turned the globe app, found the latitude line, and let it run across the Atlantic. It crossed the map above the whole United States, above every state except Alaska and Hawaii, above the Canadian border, above everything. "London lies at about 51.5 degrees north," he read off the screen. "That's farther north than any point in the contiguous United States. Farther north than the whole US-Canada border."

"No," Levi said.

"Look at the line."

Levi looked for a long time. "That can't be right. It's rainy there, not frozen."

"Exactly," Lara said, tapping the red ribbon on the wall. "That's the whole point of our station."

The point was the point, but Cole still could not feel it. He stood in front of the map while the first visitors drifted in, and the red road ran from the warm Gulf toward that impossibly high latitude, and somewhere between the road and the rainy city the warmth had to arrive. He understood the sentences. He could not yet stand there and say them as if they were his.

At ten, Ms. Holloway appeared with her clipboard, and a cluster of sixth graders in green shirts gathered in front of the map. Lara went first, smooth and quick: warm water, moving north and east, heat released to the air, westerly winds carrying it over land. Levi went second and stumbled on "westerly," saying "westernly" twice, and a sixth grader giggled, and Levi flushed to his ears. Then Ms. Holloway said, "Cole," and the small crowd turned to him.

His mouth went dry. He had a presentiment, sudden and physical, that he was about to say nothing at all, that he would stand there while the green shirts fidgeted and Ms. Holloway wrote something sad on her clipboard. Then he made himself point at the red line.

"Follow this," he said. "It starts hot, down here, and it carries the heat uphill, basically. And here's the part that got me this morning." He pulled up the latitude line on his phone and held it out flat against the wall map, letting the sixth graders crowd close. "London is up here. Fifty-one point five degrees north. That's farther north than any point in the contiguous United States. Farther north than the US border with Canada."

"Whoa," said the sixth grader who had laughed at Levi. "So London's higher than Canada?"

"Higher than the border," Cole said. "Everything in the lower forty-eight is below it." He swept his hand along the latitude line, then slid it back down to the red ribbon. "So heat has to travel a long way north to reach it. This current is the delivery."

"Like a radiator," the sixth grader said.

Cole had not thought of a radiator. He hesitated, because he wanted to say yes and he was not sure it was clean. "Sort of. A radiator makes heat. This one just moves heat that was already made somewhere else."

Ms. Holloway asked one more question, about where the heat went once the water cooled, and Cole traced the blue ribbons looping south, and admitted he was still shaky on that return loop. She marked something on her clipboard and did not show it to him.

After the sixth graders dispersed, Levi sat down against the wall with his water bottle. "Westernly," he said. "Kill me."

"You got them looking, though. They laughed, and then they looked."

Lara was already scheming about the afternoon shift, about dragging more visitors over by starting with the latitude trick, the border, the surprise. Cole looked at the map again and found that the road had not changed, only he had. Something nascent in him, a way of standing in front of a thing and asking it questions instead of memorizing its answers, was still fragile, still new, and he did not trust it yet. He knew he had explained a current, and he knew, too, that the map kept looping past the edge of the wall, off into water no one had drawn, and that he would have to keep following it.

He copied the latitude number onto the back of his hand, where he could see it, and went to refill Levi's bottle at the fountain down the hall.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, a landlord may collect a rent deposit of no more than one month's rent, or one rent period if rent is paid more often, but may not charge a damage deposit.
story:
Savannah spread the two leases across the kitchen table, weighting their corners with a bag of flour and her mother's old canning jar, because the window above the sink had been letting in a draft all week that curled paper like a hand. She had promised Victor she would have an answer by tonight, and she had promised herself something less definite: that she would actually understand the answer before she gave it.

The first lease was for a one-bedroom above the laundromat on Carling, nine hundred a month plus hydro. The second was Leticia's proposal, a shared two-bedroom near campus, six-fifty each, all utilities included except internet. Savannah had made a grid on the back of a grocery receipt. Under the first she wrote hydro, maybe eighty, and heat, unknown, and the laundromat's dryer rumbling through the floor like weather. Under the second she wrote the things Leticia had said on the phone: quiet street, a landlord named Mr. Takahashi who kept bonsai on the fire escape, a cat already in residence whether they wanted one or not.

Victor arrived at seven with his skates slung over one shoulder, even though it was June, because he refused to make two trips to the car. He sat down across from her, looked at the grid, and said, "You've made it look like a math contest. Where's the part where you decide with your heart?"

"The heart doesn't pay hydro," Savannah said, and pulled the Carling lease toward him. "Look at this. He wants first and last, fine, everybody wants first and last. But then there's this line." She put her finger under it. "Four-fifty damage deposit, refundable, condition of the unit at move-in."

Victor read it twice, the way he read exam questions, as though a second pass might reveal a trick. "Is that normal?"

"My mom paid one on our place when I was little. I remember her being furious about it and paying anyway." Savannah sat back. In her memory her mother stood in a different kitchen, holding a cheque out at arm's length as if it might bite, and saying something Savannah had been too young to keep. She could not reconstruct whether her mother had been angry at the amount or at the principle, and the difference felt like it mattered now.

"Ask Mr. Takahashi," Victor said. "Leticia said he's the landlord for the other place. He'd know what's allowed."

"He's the competition. He'll trash the Carling guy."

"He keeps bonsai, Savannah. Bonsai people don't trash people."

She called Leticia anyway, because Leticia had Mr. Takahashi's number and no patience for waiting. Twenty minutes later the doorbell rang, and there he was, a small man in a linen shirt, holding a container of cherry tomatoes from his garden as an offering. He sat where Victor had been sitting, put on the reading glasses he kept folded in his collar, and went quiet over the lease in a way that almost enthralled her, the whole kitchen narrowing to the movement of his finger down the page.

"First and last is fine," he said. "One month as a rent deposit, the landlord can hold that. But this," and he tapped the four-fifty line, "a damage deposit, he cannot charge. Not in Ontario. It's not allowed, whatever the paper says." He looked up at her over the glasses. "A rent deposit, one month, yes. A damage deposit, no."

Victor, who had been eating the tomatoes straight from the container, stopped with one halfway to his mouth. "So people just lie on leases?"

"Some don't know. Some know." Mr. Takahashi turned the page back and forth, as though the paper itself might object. "You could tell him to remove it. He might. Or you might decide you like the apartment enough not to spend the summer fighting."

Savannah looked at her grid. The numbers had not changed, but they had shifted meaning, the way a word shifts when you learn its second definition. The Carling place was still cheaper in some futures and more expensive in others, and the second bedroom with Leticia was still warm and cat-adjacent, and she understood now that her mother's old fury had probably not been about the money at all, though she would never confirm it, because her mother would only say, "We survived, didn't we?" and change the subject. There was something atavistic in that refusal, inherited like the shape of her hands, and Savannah caught herself wanting to inherit it anyway, cheque held at arm's length, the whole small war fought before breakfast.

"He also wants me to sign by Friday," she said.

"Then you have until Friday," Mr. Takahashi said. He stacked his tomatoes, stood, and paused at the door with his hand on the frame. "For the record, I charge first and last, and nothing else. But don't take my word because of that."

After he left, Victor slid the Carling lease back toward her and turned the grocery receipt over to its blank side. "So," he said, handing her the pen. "What are you going to write to him?"

Savavana looked at the line for a long moment, then printed across the top of the blank side, in letters she made deliberately even: "Remove the damage deposit and I'll consider it."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there is little time to change scenery or introduce many people.
story:
Jacob had claimed the sunroom at his grandmother's house for the whole weekend, spreading his notebook across the wicker table between the ferns and the window that looked onto the hydrangeas. His assignment was due Monday: a ten-minute play about a moment from his own life, staged in front of Ms. Harper's drama class. He had drafted eleven pages already, and every page moved somewhere new. The play opened at the lake in June, cut to the parking lot of the grocery store, jumped to Rayne's basement in July, then to the school hallway in August, and it needed six actors besides himself, which was a problem, because the class had exactly that many people in it and one of them, Eugene, refused to play anyone who cried.

"You cannot stage a whole summer," Rayne said on Saturday afternoon, leaning over the notebook with a glass of his grandmother's lemonade. "Look at this. Scene four is at the bus depot. Where are you going to get a bus?"

"It's a chair. The chair is the bus."

"The chair is also the dock and the hospital waiting room. That chair is working very hard."

Jacob laughed, then didn't, because underneath the joke sat the actual trouble. The summer he was writing about was the one when his grandfather had his first small stroke, the one nobody had called a stroke at first, and the truth of it lived in a hundred places: the porch where his grandfather kept insisting on watering the tomatoes, the car on the drive to the specialist, the kitchen where his grandmother sat with the insurance papers and said the word annuity like it was a person who owed her money. All of it felt necessary. All of it wouldn't fit.

His grandmother came through with a plate of sliced peaches and set it down without comment, the way she did when she suspected boys were hungry but would deny it. She had been an elementary school teacher for thirty-one years, and though she never offered advice unless asked, she had a way of hovering at the edge of a conversation that functioned as an invitation.

"Grandma, did you ever do theater?"

"Every spring. Fourth graders are natural actors because they don't know yet that other people are watching." She pulled a chair close to Rayne, not to Jacob, which he recognized as tact, since the notebook was on his side of the table. "What's yours about?"

"A summer. Our summer. It has six locations."

She took a peach slice and ate it slowly. "When we did plays, the short ones, we kept everyone on the same porch. Children panic if the world keeps changing around them." She said it mildly, as if reporting a fact about weather, and went back inside.

Rayne tapped the page. "She's right, and you already knew it. A ten-minute play usually has one setting and few characters, because there's no time to change scenery or introduce a whole crowd. Ms. Harper said that the first day. You were drawing your notebook cover."

"I was designing my notebook cover," Jacob said, with incipient dignity, though he could feel it collapsing even as he said it.

That evening, after Rayne went home and Eugene texted twice to expostulate about the crying clause in his contract, Jacob sat alone in the sunroom and read his own pages the way a stranger would. The lake scenes were pretty. The parking lot was tense. But the scene that made his chest hurt was the small one, page nine, two characters on the porch: his grandfather in the green chair insisting the tomatoes would die without him, and Jacob lying, saying he'd water them every morning, both of them knowing it was a lie and both accepting it anyway. Nothing else in the eleven pages did that.

He wrote at the top of a clean page: ONE SETTING. THE PORCH. TWO PEOPLE. Then he hesitated, because compressing the summer felt like a betrayal of all the other true things, the drive to the specialist, his grandmother and her papers. He couldn't claim he'd solved that. He only knew that the porch held more than the rest combined, and that a play about everything would be a play about nothing.

On Monday, Eugene arrived at school having read the new draft overnight. "I'm the grandfather," he announced in the hallway. "And I don't cry in it. I just sit in the chair and argue about tomatoes."

"That's the whole part," Jacob said.

"Good," said Eugene, and carried the chair to center stage.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: In Mark 2:27, Jesus says that the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath, answering critics of his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath.
story:
The church basement smelled of coffee and mimeograph fluid, though nobody had run a mimeograph in thirty years, and William folded his debate outline into smaller and smaller squares while Ms. Cheung arranged the chairs in a circle. The topic for Thursday's interfaith debate night was printed on the flyer she'd taped to the fellowship hall door: whether an ancient religious rule still binds modern life, argued from the text itself. William had drawn the Sabbath, which meant he had drawn the shortest straw in the group.

"You could argue from convenience," Atticus said, dropping into the chair beside him. "Nobody keeps it the old way anymore, so it's basically dead." He said it with a nonchalant wave toward the flyer, as if the argument were a coat he could take or leave. "Easy win."

William didn't answer, because Liliane was already leaning across the circle. She wanted the trophy from Thursday night, the small brass one that sat on Ms. Cheung's shelf between a dead plant and a box of communion cups, and she had wanted it since she lost last year's debate by two points. "Convenience isn't an argument," she said. "It's a surrender. If you can't show the rule is wrong from inside the rule, you haven't shown anything."

That was the problem, William thought, the actual problem. He could argue that Sunday soccer practice was reasonable, that his own grandfather objected to it on principle and stood at the kitchen window every Sunday morning watching boys carry cleats past the church like contraband. But reasonable wasn't the same as grounded. His grandfather would hear a convenience argument and close his ears, and William wanted, more than he had admitted to anyone, to be heard by him.

Ms. Cheung gave them each a Bible and a concordance and forty minutes, then went to answer the phone in the office. Liliane flipped to Exodus immediately, to the commandment itself, reading aloud the words about keeping the day holy and doing no work. "The rule is absolute," she said. "That's my side. You'll lose."

William turned pages without a plan, following the cross-references the way he followed creek tributaries in summer, just to see where they went. In Mark, chapter two, he stopped. The disciples were picking grain on the Sabbath, and critics had objected, and he read the reply twice, then a third time, because he couldn't quite believe the shape of it. "The Sabbath was made for man," he said slowly, "and not man for the Sabbath." He looked up. "Did you know that's in there?"

Atticus came around the table to read it over his shoulder. "So the rule itself contains its own limit?"

"Or its own purpose," Liliane said, but her voice had changed; she was no longer performing confidence. She copied the verse onto an index card, then sat turning it in her fingers. "That's harder to beat than convenience."

They spent the rest of the hour building the case, or trying to. William made himself argue Liliane's side too, out loud, pacing between the coffee urn and the piano, because Ms. Cheung had told them once that a debater who can't state the opposing case has only verisimilitude, the appearance of argument, not its substance. He could feel where his case held and where it didn't. The verse said what it said, plainly. But it didn't say whether picking grain and playing soccer were the same kind of thing, and it didn't say who got to decide what the Sabbath was for.

When Ms. Cheung came back, William tried to verbalize the position he was assembling: that the rule might still bind, but as an instrument rather than a cage, ordered toward something human rather than against it. The sentence came out crooked, and he tried again, and a third time, and she let him keep struggling without rescuing him.

That Sunday, his grandfather stood at the window as usual, and William, cleats in hand, paused on the porch. "In Mark two," he said, "when the disciples picked grain on the Sabbath, Jesus told the critics the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath." He hadn't planned to say it there, in the doorway, with the church bell three blocks away starting up. His grandfather looked at him for a long moment, then at the cleats.

"Made for man," his grandfather repeated. "And you think kicking a ball is what it was made for?"

William shifted his weight on the step. "I think that's the question," he said. "I really don't know the answer yet."

His grandfather turned the idea over the way he turned a wrench, slowly, testing the threads. "Ask your coach if practice can start at one instead of ten," he said finally, and pulled the door shut behind him.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is treated as a fallacy in formal debate.
story:
Alex had taped a hand-drawn timer above the kitchen table, a paper clock with a red wedge marked cinco minutos, and every evening after dinner he sat beneath it and argued with the toaster. The topic was whether schools should be a meritocracy, and the language was Spanish, which he had studied for exactly three years and could read far better than he could speak. His mother dried dishes behind him and occasionally offered the word she remembered from her own night class, which was "baño," and which fit no argument ever devised.

The trouble was not vocabulary. He could assemble the words, slowly, like furniture with an instruction sheet. The trouble was that a debate is a kind of running, and he was walking with a dictionary on his back. When he tried to say that ranking students by results sounds fair but rewards those with tutors and quiet houses, the sentence collapsed halfway and he stood in the wreckage saying "pero, pero, pero" until the paper clock seemed to smirk at him.

Khadija arrived on Thursday with her laptop and her own agenda. She wanted Alex as her partner at the regional tournament in March, in the category where the entire round was conducted in the target language, and she had decided this without, strictly, asking him. She set up her laptop across the table, opened a spreadsheet titled ALEX (PROGRESS?), and said, "Okay. Debate me. You're for the meritocracy side tonight, so you can't hide behind complaining about inequality. You have to defend the thing."

Larissa came for the snacks, officially, and for the company, actually, but she had a talent for cruelty so precise it functioned as a teaching tool. She leaned on the counter eating the good crackers and listened while Alex, sweating, constructed his opening: that rewarding achievement gives everyone a clear ladder, que todos pueden subir, that the ladder is not the same as the starting line. Then she said, sweetly, "Hard to take that seriously from a guy whose accent turns ' meritocracia' into a small explosion."

The kitchen went quiet except for the radiator, which chose that moment to clang like a struck bell. Alex felt the remark land and, before he could be hurt by it, noticed something odd, which was that his argument had not been touched at all. The accent and the ladder had nothing to do with each other. Larissa had simply moved the fight to a different street. Khadija pointed at her with a cracker of her own and said, "Ad hominem. You attacked him instead of the point. In formal debate that's a fallacy, she gets nothing for it."

"That's ad hominem," Larissa agreed, delighted, dusting salt from her fingers. "I did it on purpose. Priya tried it on me at the last tournament and the judge wrote it on the ballot. I wanted to see if Alex would fold." He had not folded, he realized, because for five full seconds he had been too busy thinking about ladders to think about his own voice, and in those seconds the Spanish had come out whole. It was a discovery with a ridiculous shape: mockery as medicine, insults as physical therapy. He felt as though some argumentative muscle, strained all season, had begun to convalesce.

Ms. Jung from next door knocked at seven with a plate of coriander-heavy dumplings, as she did whenever the smells through the wall suggested teenagers were feeding themselves badly. She had grown up in a household that switched between three languages depending on which grandmother was speaking, and she refused to be impressed by anyone's Spanish until it survived an interruption. So she sat down, took Khadija's side of the meritocracy question without apology, and began asking questions in a quick, mercurial way that changed direction every time Alex found his footing. Once she interrupted him mid-sentence to ask whether the tea was oolong or jasmine, then returned to his argument exactly where he had left it, and he discovered he could pick the thread back up, "como decía," he said, like a man setting down a suitcase and lifting it again.

When the paper clock's red wedge had been survived for the third time in a row, Khadija closed the laptop without recording anything and said, "March. You and me. Say yes in Spanish." Alex said he would think about it, and she said that was not one of the allowed answers, and Ms. Jung poured the last of the tea into his cup as though to seal some contract she had not been told about. Larissa reached across the table and stole the final cracker, holding it up like a trophy. "Five minutes," she said. "You only have to not explode for five minutes."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Canada's 2019 food guide suggests filling half the plate with vegetables and fruits, a quarter with protein foods and a quarter with whole grain foods.
story:
Oliver stood in front of the open refrigerator on Sunday morning and counted what his mother had left behind before her night shift: half a bag of carrots, three eggs, a jar of mustard, and a takeout container of rice gone hard at the edges. She had left forty dollars under the fruit bowl, which was generous and also a diagnosis. In September he would be in a residence with a shared kitchen, and if he could not turn forty dollars into seven dinners, the semester would begin with a lot of instant noodles and quiet regret.

He commandeered the kitchen table, pushing aside his mother's unopened mail, and drew a grid on the back of an envelope: seven columns, one for each day. Then he stopped, because he did not actually know what a week of meals looked like. At home, food appeared. At school, Mr. Marino, who lived two floors down and taught health, had once mentioned something about a plate during a fire drill of all things, something Oliver had half heard while watching the stairwell. He texted Wade instead, who was already at college and insufferable about it.

"plate thing," Wade typed back. "canada's 2019 food guide. half the plate vegetables and fruits, a quarter protein foods, a quarter whole grain foods. i have it tattooed on my brain from mr marino's class."

Oliver read it twice. Half vegetables and fruits. A quarter protein foods. A quarter whole grain foods. It was so simple it felt like cheating, and then, as he stared at his grid, it started to feel like architecture. He did not need recipes; he needed proportions. He could make one big pot of something on Sunday and another on Wednesday, split it into containers, and every meal would still be a plate if he kept the ratios in his head. He wrote at the top of the envelope: half veg/fruit, quarter protein, quarter whole grain, and underneath, a shopping list arranged by section of the store.

At the supermarket he moved slowly, comparing prices per gram like a man twice his age. Frozen vegetables were cheaper than fresh and would survive his schedule. A bag of brown rice, a few cans of chickpeas, one whole chicken that the cashier would not have to butcher because it was already cut into pieces. He ran into Dennis in the pasta aisle, holding two boxes and looking paralyzed.

"Bro," Dennis said. "White or whole wheat. My mom always bought white and I don't know anything."

"Whole grain," Oliver said. "Quarter of the plate. The rest is vegetables and protein. That's the whole system, basically." He held up his envelope, the list smudged but legible, and Dennis took a photo of it with the seriousness of someone documenting evidence.

Back home, Oliver roasted the chicken with carrots and onions, boiled the rice, and portioned everything into containers his mother had saved from takeout, washed and stacked for years in the cupboard, an encapsulation of her own quiet foresight he had never once appreciated. He stacked the containers in the fridge in rows, Monday through Sunday, and photographed that too, sending it to Wade without comment.

The week taught him things the envelope had not. Tuesday's vegetables went limp by Thursday, which is how he learned that some meals are evanescent and must be scheduled early, while rice and chickpeas hold. On Wednesday his mother came home at midnight, saw the fridge full of labeled containers, and stood there with her coat still on. She took the Wednesday one, microwaved it, and ate standing at the counter while he pretended to be asleep and listened to her fork against the plate. On Friday Mr. Marino caught him carrying recycling down the chute and said the smell of roasted chicken had been drifting into the hallway all week, and that if Oliver ever wanted to talk about the plate thing in more detail, his door was open. Oliver said maybe, honestly uncertain, because he still did not know whether he had learned to cook or only to portion, whether the system was a philosophy or just a trick for surviving.

Saturday morning his mother left forty dollars under the fruit bowl again, but this time with a note: "chicken again?" Oliver stood at the table with a fresh envelope and a pen, and drew the grid. He wrote at the top, half, quarter, quarter, and then, after a pause, added one word beneath the list: "lentils?"

"So we're doing this every week now?" his mother asked from the doorway, coat half on, keys in her fist.

"Every week," he said, and clicked the pen.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
story:
Annabelle had postponed the lesson twice already, once for a dentist appointment she did not actually have, and so when the rain started at four o'clock she made herself walk to the driving school anyway, her letter of resignation from the swim team folded in her back pocket like a confession she hadn't mailed. The school occupied a strip mall between a nail salon and a place that sold vacuum cleaners, and its waiting room smelled of burnt coffee and laminated paper. A poster on the wall said CONFIDENT DRIVERS ARE MADE, NOT BORN, which Annabelle found faintly threatening.

"You're my six o'clock," said Ms. Yamamoto, a compact woman with gray-streaked hair and a dour expression that Annabelle would later learn concealed a dry sense of humor. "The one who canceled twice."

"I had a dentist thing."

"Of course you did." Ms. Yamamoto held up a set of keys. "Rain's good for you. Rain is honest. Sunlight lets you believe you're better than you are."

Before the lesson, Annabelle sat in the plastic chair by the window and read the message her friend Jayce had sent that afternoon: "ok so i know you quit swim and i'm not going to give you a speech about it, but i want you to know that i taped your split times from regionals inside my locker, which is either a compliment or harassment, haven't decided. also if you crash the car tonight please leave me your hoodie in your will." She was still smiling at it when Ms. Yamamoto beckoned her out to a white sedan with a STUDENT DRIVER sign bolted to its roof like a scarlet letter.

The first half hour was unremarkable, which Annabelle counted as a triumph. She checked her mirrors, feathered the brake at a stop sign, and only stalled twice, and Ms. Yamamoto said "adequate" in a tone that Annabelle was beginning to understand was her highest available praise. The rain thickened as dusk came down. Streetlights smeared yellow across the wet asphalt, and the wipers kept their patient metronome.

"Turn left up here," Ms. Yamamoto said. "There's a dip in the road that collects water when it rains like this. Just drive through it."

The dip was deeper than it looked, a broad shallow lake stretching across the whole lane, and the instant the tires entered it the steering went weightless in Annabelle's hands, as if the wheel had been disconnected from the car. Her instinct was to brake hard and wrench the wheel toward dry pavement. Instead, because some corner of her mind recalled a line from the handbook she'd read at one in the morning, she eased her foot off the accelerator. She didn't brake, didn't steer, just let the car slow itself. A second passed, maybe two, and then the tires found the road again and the steering went solid, and she was through, breathing hard, hands cramped at ten and two.

"What was that?" she asked.

"Water built up between the tires and the road. The car lost traction. Ease off the accelerator and the tires can get their grip back." Ms. Yamamoto was watching her, the dour face almost interested. "You could have panicked. Why didn't you?"

Annabelle considered lying, then didn't. "I don't know. I read it somewhere. I didn't actually think it would work." She realized, saying it, that this was a philosophy she'd been living for months without naming: do the reasonable thing with no faith whatsoever that it will help, and then be stunned when it does. Quitting swim had felt like the opposite, like slamming the brakes and spinning the wheel, and she still couldn't decide which approach the last two years of her life had proven correct. Maybe both. Maybe neither. Maybe it depended on the road.

"Pull over at the gas station," Ms. Yamamoto said. "We'll switch seats and you can tell me why a girl who reads the handbook at one in the morning thinks she can't do anything."

In the passenger seat, wipers still sweeping, Annabelle took the folded letter out of her pocket and showed her the first line, and then, when Ms. Yamamoto only raised an eyebrow, texted Jayce instead: "did not crash. the car floated for a second like a swan and then it didn't. also i think i understand something but i'll need you to explain it back to me tomorrow because i don't trust my own sagacity." She was still typing when Ms. Yamamoto pulled out of the gas station and said, "Good. Now, one more thing. Never tell the insurance company you read the handbook at one in the morning. It does not exonerate you."

"The swan floats," Annabelle said, mostly to herself, watching the rain collect in the dip behind them. "The swan floats, and then it doesn't."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java fields left uninitialized get default values: 0 for numbers, false for booleans, and null for object references.
story:
Elijah arrived at coding club eleven minutes late, which by his own arithmetic meant he had technically arrived early for the part he cared about. Mr. Bakker had promised that today they would finally stop writing everything in main and build a real class, private fields and all, and Elijah had spent the walk from the bus rehearsing a mental image of himself as someone who already knew how to do that. The reality was a lab that smelled of whiteboard marker and someone's leftover noodles, and Maika already at a terminal, waving him over with the impatience of a person who has saved a seat and regrets it.
