"Where were you?" she said. "Eamon's been giving a peroration on why semicolons should be optional. It's been very long and very unpersuasive."

"I was debilitated," Elijah said, dropping into the chair. "By gym."

"You walked here."

"Gym debilitates the spirit as well as the body. It lingers."

Eamon spun his chair around. "Anyway, Bakker's giving us the whole period. We build a class, we write a test, and if it works, we get to leave the sandbox behind forever. I'm thinking a Monster class. For a game. Every serious programmer starts with monsters."

"I was thinking a Cat," Maika said.

"Cats are monsters with better publicity."

Mr. Bakker, who had been pretending not to listen from the front of the room, said without turning around, "Whatever you build, the fields are private, and the only way in is through getters. If I see a public field I will assume you have learned nothing and grade you accordingly, in my heart, where it counts." He wrote on the whiteboard in glacial, deliberate strokes: private String name; private int health; private boolean alive. "The constructor is yours to figure out. That's the interesting part."

They figured out the boring part first. Elijah typed the class skeleton while Maika narrated, which mostly consisted of her saying "curly brace" every time he forgot one, and Eamon proposed increasingly elaborate monster abilities that would have debilitated their grade point average if implemented. The Cat faction won on the grounds that a Cat needed only a name and health, and health could start at nine. "Nine lives," Maika said. "It's canonical." Eamon conceded with the air of a man losing a battle to win the war, since his name was still going on the file.

The Cat class came together quickly, which should have warned them. Private fields, check. A getter for the name, check. A getter for health, check. Eamon, who had appointed himself test writer because it let him avoid doing anything else, opened a test class and wrote a Cat, then printed its name to the console so they could all admire their work. "Behold," he said, gesturing at the screen like a magician revealing the empty hat.

The console printed: null.

They sat with it for a moment. "That's not a cat," Maika said. "That's the ghost of a cat. You've written code that summons the absence of a cat."

"It's not null because it's broken," Elijah said slowly, scrolling back through the class. He had expected an error, red text, the machine shouting at him, the usual. Null felt different, quieter, like the program had answered a question he hadn't asked. He read the constructor again, line by line, and the line-by-line was the problem, or rather the missing line. They had written a constructor that took a name and set the health to nine, and then, in the rush of curly braces and Eamon's commentary, they had never actually assigned the name. The parameter just sat there, unused, like a guest nobody spoke to at a party.

"So it never set it," Maika said. "But then why isn't the name an error? Why null?"

"Because it has to be something," Elijah said. He was reasoning aloud now, and he could feel the two halves of his brain arriving from different directions, the half that wanted the machine to be strict and the half that was starting to see why it wasn't. "Java doesn't leave a field empty. If you never set it, numbers just start at 0, booleans start at false, and anything that's an object, like a String, starts at null. So the Cat exists, it has health, it's alive, it just has no name, because we never gave it one."

Eamon frowned. "So it's a nine-health cat with no name."

"With nine health and no name," Elijah said, and then, because it was irresistible, "a cat with no name gets null. It's like the cat's been neutered by the compiler."

Eamon laughed so hard he knocked his water bottle into his lap, which everyone agreed served him right. Maika, meanwhile, was already typing at speed. "If it's alive we can print that too," she said, adding a getter for the boolean and calling it in the test. They ran it again. The health printed 9. The alive printed true. The name printed null, stubbornly, correctly, a little monument to the line they'd forgotten. It struck Elijah as almost generous of the language, the way it handed you a default instead of a scolding, though he could also see the other side of it, that a silent default could hide a mistake for weeks if you weren't watching the console. He filed both opinions away side by side without deciding between them, which felt, for once, like a kind of progress.

The fix took one line. Elijah added the assignment in the constructor, saved, ran the test, and this time the console printed: Whiskers. Eamon stood and took a bow to an audience of two. Mr. Bakker drifted past their terminal, looked at the output, looked at the test, and said, "Congratulations. You've invented a named cat." He moved on before Elijah could tell whether that was praise.

"Next week," Eamon said, wringing water out of his sleeve, "the Monster class. It has a weakness field, and if you forget to set it, it defaults to zero weaknesses, which is actually the strongest possible monster."

"That's not how any of this works," Maika said.

"Prove it," said Eamon, and reached for the keyboard.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
William had the sample ballot folded into quarters in his back pocket, and he had been carrying it for six days like a receipt he kept meaning to return.

He sat at the kitchen table on a Tuesday morning in November, home from school because the district gave Election Day off, which struck him as a joke, since most of the students who got the day off could not vote. His grandfather was at the stove, burning butter in a pan with the calm of a man who believed burnt butter was a flavor. On the counter sat the grandfather's coffee mug, chipped at the rim, with a faded flag printed on it and the words OLD ENOUGH TO FIGHT, OLD ENOUGH TO VOTE running around the outside in gold letters that time had dulled.

"You're staring at my mug," his grandfather said, without turning around.

"I'm staring at your mug," William admitted. "It sounds like an ad for a gym."

His grandfather laughed, a short sound, and turned the flame down. "That was the slogan. When they lowered the voting age to eighteen. Because eighteen-year-olds could get drafted for Vietnam. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. That's how the argument went."

"Wait." William pulled the folded ballot out of his pocket and set it on the table between them like evidence. "So I can vote because of a war?"

"Because of a war nobody my age wanted," his grandfather said. "Two of the guys in my high school class went. One came back." He slid the eggs onto a plate and sat down across from William, and for a while neither of them said anything, because there was nothing wry available and both of them knew it.

William had spent the fall telling anyone who asked, mostly Reagan and Annabelle, who asked constantly, that he wasn't sure he saw the point. One vote among millions, a number so large it made his single ballot feel like a raindrop volunteering for the ocean. Reagan had called this "a coward's math," which was rich coming from someone who had registered to vote on her eighteenth birthday and then spent forty minutes at the polling place in 2019, during a local race, photographing the machine for her social media. Annabelle had taken a different approach. She had gone quiet and said, "My grandmother couldn't vote until she was thirty-one," and then changed the subject to cafeteria fries, and William had understood that the conversation was over without anyone conceding anything.

Now he looked at the mug again. The logic of the slogan was blunt enough that it embarrassed him slightly, the way simple things did. Somebody had decided that if you were old enough to be conscripted and shipped across the world and shot at, you were old enough to check a box. The vote had not been handed down from some pedagogue on a mountain; it had been dragged out of an argument about who owed what to whom. His grandfather, nineteen in a different century, had been eligible for a draft that William would never face, and the ballot in William's pocket was, in some way William could not quite phrase, the receipt for that.

"I told Reagan I probably wouldn't bother," William said. "Today. She's going to text me."

"So bother," his grandfather said. "Or don't. The eggs are getting cold either way." He ate in the unconcerned way of a man who had watched many elections come and go and had voted in most of them, including, William suddenly suspected, a few he would not want discussed at this table.

William ate his eggs. He thought about his uncle, who liked to say at Thanksgiving that the whole system was rigged by men in suits and that voting was a loyalty card for the destitute of spirit, which had sounded sophisticated when William was fourteen and now sounded like someone burnishing his own cynicism until it shone enough to hide behind. His uncle had never, as far as William knew, missed an election either. Everyone at that table performed their indifference carefully, and then went and voted anyway, except William, who had performed his earnestness for months and was the only one sitting at home at ten in the morning with an unfolded sample ballot and a decision he had been pretending was philosophical when it was mostly inertia.

He did the dishes, which surprised his grandfather into raising one eyebrow, and then he put on his jacket. At the door he stopped, went back to the counter, and picked up the mug to look at it one more time, turning it so the gold letters caught the window light.

"Can I take this?" he said. "To the polling place. For luck."

"It's a mug, not a rabbit's foot," his grandfather said. But he washed it out quickly under the tap, dried it on his shirt, and handed it over.

William walked the four blocks to the school gym with the mug wrapped in a plastic bag in one hand and his ballot in the other, and when Reagan texted him a single question mark, he photographed the gym doors and sent it without any caption at all.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Herman and Chomsky's second filter is advertising: outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away.
story:
Eva spread the two newspapers across the study table in the library, aligning their edges the way she aligned everything when she was nervous. On the left, the front page of the Ridgefield Courier, where a story about the new waterfront development ran under a headline that read Plans Praised as Windfall for Harbor. On the right, the draft of her own story for the school paper, the Halloway Herald, which described the same development as a hazard to the salt marsh, and named the developer, and named his company, and named the fact that his company bought a full-page ad in the Courier every week. The Herald went to print at midnight. It was four o'clock.

Lorelai dropped into the chair across from her with a phone held out like evidence. "Read this," she said. "It's from Mr. Doran. The guy who owns Doran's Marine. He buys a quarter page in every issue of ours." Eva read the message twice. Doran's Marine, it said, would pull its advertising if the story about the harbor ran, because the developer was a customer of his, and he did not pay the paper to make his customers look bad. Below the message, Lorelai had typed and deleted three replies, all of them visible as gray ghosts.

"That ad money pays for the printing," Lorelai said. "Half of it, maybe more. Marley's counting it now." Across the reading room, Marley was bent over a ledger at the circulation desk, where Mr. Mensah had let them set up camp after closing hours approached, on the condition that they keep their voices down and their chips away from the returned books. He was reshelving biographies a few aisles off, unhurried, occasionally glancing over with the mild attention of a man who had supervised teenagers long enough to know when to intervene and when not to.

"We could soften it," Eva said, and heard how the sentence fell, like something dropped. "Cut his name. Keep the marsh." Lorelai remonstrated, quietly, because of Mr. Mensah's rule, but firmly: the name was the story. Without the name, the hazard simply existed, causeless, like weather. Eva argued back, and then stopped arguing, because she noticed that Lorelai's hands were shaking slightly, and remembered that Lorelai's mother worked at the marine supply counter at Doran's from March to October, and that October had not yet come.

Marley arrived at the table with the ledger and a face like a verdict. "If he pulls out, we can print eight pages instead of twelve. Or we run his ad as the back page and the front page says nothing about the harbor." She sat down hard. "Or we find another way to pay for paper."

Eva got up and walked, because sitting had become impossible. In the stacks she passed Mr. Mensah, who was pushing a cart of donated books, and on the cart, spine up, she saw a fat, dull-colored paperback with a title she half recognized: Manufacturing Consent. She had seen it cited somewhere, in a footnote she had skipped. She pulled it off the cart and stood in the aisle turning pages until she found the chapter called something like a propaganda model, and within it a list. Five filters, the book said, through which money shaped what counted as news. The second filter was advertising. Outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away. She read it twice. It was not a scandal. It was a mechanism, quiet as plumbing.

She carried the book back to the table, set it down open, and said, "Look. Second filter. Advertising." Lorelai read, frowning. Marley read, and said, "So it's not just Doran being a jerk. It's the whole pipe. Any paper that lives on ad money has a reason to dodge stories that scare the advertisers off. Even us. Especially us, we're tiny." Eva nodded, slowly, because a strange relief was moving through her, the kind that comes from learning that a private trouble is also a public law. It did not solve anything. She was honest with herself about that. The book did not say what a small paper with a midnight deadline ought to do. It only said why the choice kept arriving.

Mr. Mensah appeared at the table with the reshelving cart and looked at the open book, then at the three of them, and said nothing, because he was a librarian and not a pedagogue, and he believed that some discoveries should be allowed to settle without commentary. Instead he said, "There is a copier that takes coins, and a display case by the entrance that is empty this month. Also, I am told the historical society has wanted someone to archive the marsh photographs for two years." He took the chips off the returned books and moved on.

They worked until the library's lamps went amber. Marley built a new budget on the back of the ledger, penciling in coin donations, a print run of eight pages, a donation button Lorelai would code before eleven. Eva cut two paragraphs she loved, kept the developer's name, and wrote a small box at the bottom of the front page: how the Herald was funded, how much Doran's Marine had paid, and that it had asked them to stop. Marley proofread the box three times. At eleven forty, Lorelai's mother called; Lorelai stepped into the stairwell, and came back six minutes later, pale, and said only, "She says print it."

Eva hit send on the final pages at 11:58. Then she turned to the window, where beyond the parking lot the harbor lay black and motionless, pelagic even here, at the edge of town, keeping the marsh and the pilings and whatever was coming next beneath its flat dark surface. Lorelai stood beside her. "Whatever happens with Doran," Eva said, "next month we run the follow-up." Lorelai put a coin on the windowsill, heads up, for luck, and went to get her coat.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
The article was four paragraphs long and printed on blue paper, and Ms. Buchanan had said the summaries would start on Wednesday, in Spanish, in front of everyone. Alexa had promised herself she would not be the one standing there silent. She sat in the library corner after last period with the page flat under the lamp, running her finger under the first sentence of the third paragraph, where the trouble was.

The article was about a dispute over a river, or a road, or possibly a school; her vocabulary was still thin enough that whole clauses slid past her like weather. But the fourth paragraph contained the word "según," and after it, a claim so bold it startled her: that the town's water had been safe all along. She copied the sentence into her notebook and translated it as fact. The water had been safe. That was what the paper said.

She found Mohammed at the table by the windows, his own blue page folded into quarters.

"What's yours about?" he asked.

"A river. Contamination. Except the water was actually safe, apparently."

Mohammed frowned at her notebook. "Mine says the opposite. Mine says the tests found something."

"That can't both be right."

They compared articles. His was from a different paper, three days later, and it did not say the water was safe. It said a company official had said the water was safe. Alexa read her sentence again, slower, and saw the shape of it: the claim sat behind "según" the way a voice sits behind a door.

"It means 'according to,'" Asher said, dropping into the chair beside her, backpack first. He had spent a summer with his grandmother in Bogotá and liked to let everyone know it. "Spanish news writers use it constantly. Según the minister, según the study. It tells you who's talking."

"So it's not the reporter saying the water was safe," Alexa said. "It's the company saying it."

"Right. The reporter isn't vouching. The reporter is reporting."

Alexa looked at the sentence she had written in her notebook, the clean little translation she had been proud of, and felt the floor of it give way. She had taken a claim and made it a fact without noticing the difference. Mohammed leaned over her page and tapped the word.

"So I have to say who said it," Alexa said. "In the summary. Otherwise I'd be putting words in the reporter's mouth."

"If the summary's supposed to be honest, yeah."

Wednesday came faster than she wanted. Ms. Buchanan called names in a strange order, alphabet backwards, so Alexa went third instead of near the end, and she stood with her notes even though she had promised herself she wouldn't need them. Her first two sentences came out flat but grammatical, and she could hear Asher not laughing, which helped. Then she reached the claim.

"Según la empresa," she said, and stopped, because the next part mattered. "La empresa dice que el agua estaba segura." The company says the water was safe. She heard herself add the attribution like a handrail, and heard the difference it made. A claim with a source was a different object from a fact, lighter, movable, owned by someone.

"Good," Ms. Buchanan said. "Why did you say 'dice' there instead of just 'estaba'?"

"Because the article doesn't say the water was safe. It says the company said it. The 'según' marks it."

Ms. Buchanan's mouth did something small that might have been approval. She made a note on her clipboard and called the next name.

Afterward, in the corridor, Mohammed caught up with her. "So which paper was right? Yours or mine?"

"Neither, maybe. Both of them were just writing down who said what." Alexa slung her bag over her shoulder. "The tests are the fact. The articles are the claims."

"Then how do we find out about the tests?"

"I don't know yet." She pushed open the door to the stairwell, holding it for him with her hip. "Según somebody, probably."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Ray Oldenburg's 1989 book The Great Good Place named 'third places', such as cafes and libraries, where people meet outside home and work.
story:
The moving truck had left two days early, so Hayden rode in the family car with his father and the last boxes, watching the interstate unspool through a windshield that needed cleaning. Somewhere behind them, four hundred miles behind them, Trisha and Lachlan were probably at the diner already, taking the booth by the window without him. His father kept the radio on a station that faded in and out, and between the static he said, "Give it a month. You'll find your people."

"I had my people," Hayden said. "I had them sorted."

He hadn't, exactly, sorted them. They had accumulated, the way things do, through twelve years of shared classrooms and buses and one disastrous science camp. Nobody had decided anything. That was the part he kept turning over as the signs counted down the exits: how much of a life is chosen and how much is just where you happened to be standing. His father's new job came with a relocation package, a phrase that sounded tidy, like an annuity, money arriving on schedule whether you wanted it or not. The move arrived whether he wanted it or not. His mother had said the same thing about her own transfer years ago, and he had never once asked her what that had cost.

The new house had his boxes in it by dark. The first week he unpacked badly, then stopped, and by the second Friday he was walking to the public library after school because it was the only building in town he could enter without a reason. He chose a table near the periodicals because it had two chairs, as if expecting company, and he did his orientation paperwork there and then, when the paperwork ran out, nothing.

On the fourth afternoon a girl his age sat at the other chair without asking and spread out a calculus problem set. She didn't look up. Hayden noticed that he was holding his breath, which was absurd, and let it out slowly, and got back to his own nothing. When she left an hour later she said, "Same table tomorrow, probably," and he said, "Probably," and the word sat in his chest like something warm.

He started noticing the building itself after that. The retired men who met at the coffee machine at three and argued about the county softball standings. The woman who came in every day with a novel and left with the same novel, unread, Hayden suspected, but finished being wherever she was. He wondered whether the library was doing something for all of them that none of them was naming, some function the way a heart has a function, invisible while it works.

He found the answer by accident, which is how he preferred to find things. Shelving his father's returned books in the sociology section, a habit he'd developed because it gave his hands something to do, he pulled out a fat paperback with a cracked spine: The Great Good Place, by Ray Oldenburg, 1989. He read the first chapter standing in the aisle, one hip against the cart. Third places, the book called them. Cafes, libraries, spots like this one. Places where people meet outside home and work. First place home, second place work, third place everything that makes a town a town instead of a pile of addresses.

He texted Trisha a photo of the cover that night, from the car outside the library while his father ran into the pharmacy. "This is what the diner was," he typed. "Third place. Home, work or school, then the third one. We never called it anything." She replied with three exclamation points and then, a minute later, "Lachlan says the diner doesn't count because you have to buy fries." Hayden laughed out loud in the passenger seat, a visceral, surprising laugh, the first one since the move, and typed back that the book would disagree, and that fries were optional anyway.

But he was honest enough with himself to leave a gap in the argument. Knowing the word for something didn't build it. His father could not be handed a map of third places and told to relocate the family a second time, back toward the diner and the booth by the window. And the girl at the calculus table, whose name he still didn't know, might stop coming tomorrow, and the warm word "probably" would turn out to mean nothing at all. The book named a pattern; it didn't promise him the pattern would hold. He sat with that, the streetlight coming on over the parking lot, the pharmacy doors sliding open and shut, and found he could hold both things at once, the idea and the uncertainty, without either one breaking.

His father got back in the car with a paper bag and a receipt he put straight into his shirt pocket. "You look better," his father said, pulling out of the space. "Something happen?"

"Kind of," Hayden said, and watched the library shrink in the side mirror, its lit windows standing in the dark like proof. "Same table tomorrow. Probably."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Bernhard Riemann gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen.
story:
Room 214 smelled of dry-erase marker and the cafeteria's leftover lasagna, which drifted in whenever someone opened the door. Olivia sat at the front table with her notebook open to a page divided by a vertical line: on the left, rectangles drawn under a curve; on the right, blank space she had been avoiding for two days. The math club's regional showcase was on Saturday, and Mr. Luo had said, more than once, that the presentation needed both halves finished by Thursday's meeting.

Tristen slid into the chair beside her and tapped the right side of the page. "Still nothing?"

"I keep getting different answers," Olivia said. "If I use ten rectangles I get 3.45. With a hundred I get 3.32. With five hundred it changes again. Which one is the area? They can't all be."

"Maybe the one with more rectangles," Tristen said. "Closer to the real thing."

"But then why not a thousand? Why not infinite? There's no rectangle called 'infinite' that I can draw." She pulled the sheet of graph paper toward her and began again on the curve, y equals x squared between zero and two, the same curve Mr. Luo had assigned in September when she'd joined the club knowing nothing beyond algebra.

At the whiteboard, Naomi was printing the outline for the club's history segment. "I'm stuck too," she said without turning around. "The report's supposed to be one page on where integration comes from. I looked it up last night. Guess whose name is on the rectangle method."

"Euler," Tristen said.

"Bernhard Riemann," Naomi said. She enunciated the name carefully, the way she did with words she'd only ever read. "He gave his definition of the integral in 1854, in the paper he submitted to qualify as a lecturer at the University of Göttingen." She set the marker down. "He wrote it to get a job. That's the whole origin story."

Olivia stopped drawing. "Say that again. 1854?"

"1854. The Göttingen paper." Naomi copied the sentence onto an index card, word for word, for the citation slide.

Olivia looked at her divided page. On the left, rectangles: crude, ancient-feeling, the kind of thing Archimedes could have scratched in sand. Yet the method on the right, the one with the fancy symbols and the elongated S, carried this man's name from 1854, from a hiring paper. She had assumed the symbol came first and the rectangles were a modern teaching trick, a picture drawn afterward to help students. It was the opposite. The rectangles were the idea. The symbol was a shorthand for what happened when you let them become too many to count.

She took out a pencil. "If the rectangles keep shrinking," she said, mostly to herself, "then each one contributes almost nothing, but there are so many that the total stops changing. That has to be what the definition means. It's not a different method. It's my method, taken to the end."

Tristen leaned over. "So which number do you put in the answer box?"

"I don't put a rectangle number. I put the number they're all closing in on." She computed it, working the formula Mr. Luo had shown them the previous week, and got eight thirds. She checked her decimal answers: 3.45, 3.32, 3.33. They were converging on 2.67, on eight thirds, from both directions depending on whether her rectangles sat above or below the curve.

Mr. Luo came by on his circuit of the room, coffee cup in hand. "Olivia. Thursday deadline. Where are you?"

She turned her notebook so he could see. "Left side is the history. Riemann, 1854, the Göttingen lecture paper. Right side is the calculation. Eight thirds." She paused. "I still don't know how anyone can say the rectangles actually reach the limit. Infinite steps don't finish. Unless you just decide they do."

Mr. Luo drank his coffee and said nothing, which was his way of handing the question back.

"That's the part I can't fix," she admitted. "I can say the answer, and I can prove the decimals squeeze toward it, but whether the infinity is real or just an agreement, that I can't tell you."

"So put that in the presentation," Naomi said from the whiteboard. "The card says what Riemann did. Your part says what's still open, at least for you."

"Mr. Luo will dock points for 'unresolved.'" Tristen mimicked his voice, flat and severe: "In mathematics we demand closure."

"We demand it in physics too," Naomi said. "Every measurement determined by the last one. Whole universe as a clock." She wrote determinism on the board and then crossed it out. "But nobody's proved the universe runs that way either, and the physics still works."

Olivia copied her two columns onto a fresh sheet and taped it to the presentation board, rectangles on the left, eight thirds on the right, and beneath both a line she left in pencil rather than ink: whether the infinite sum is completed or only approached, she did not know. The clock over the door read 4:52. Eight minutes left in the meeting, four days until Saturday.

She sharpened her pencil and started tracing over the curve one more time, slow and dark, so it would show from the back of the room.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Mexico's Day of the Dead is traditionally celebrated on November 1 and 2, when families build ofrendas, or home altars, with photos and the favorite foods and drinks of relatives who have died.
story:
The car smelled of the cardboard box riding in the back seat, and of the coffee her mother had stopped drinking an hour ago, the cup sweating in the cupholder. Nicole sat behind her mother, Mustafa beside her, because his own house was on the way to the bakery and his mother had said he should go along, "for company," which in their families meant for supervision of grief. The bakery downtown was the only one that baked pan de muerto this early in October, and Nicole's mother wanted the first loaves of the season.

"Explain it again," Mustafa said. "You're building a table for a dead person."

"An altar," Nicole said. "They call them ofrendas. November first and second, Day of the Dead. You put out photos, and their favorite foods and drinks, and it's for relatives who have died. My mom wants to do it for my grandmother this year, since it's the first year."

"In the house?"

"On the sideboard. My grandmother loved that sweet bread, the one with the bones on top. Pan de muerto. That's the whole reason we're driving out here."

Her mother's eyes stayed on the road. Since the funeral she had been stoic about most things, the casseroles, the relatives, the insurance paperwork, but when she spoke about the bread her voice went thin, so Nicole had volunteered to handle it, and then had asked Mustafa to come, because she did not trust herself alone with her mother's silences yet.

At the bakery the line went out the door. Nicole waited while her mother circled the block, and Mustafa read the poster taped to the window, which showed a family arranging marigolds around a framed photograph. "It's not sad," he said. "The picture. They look like they're setting a table for someone expected."

"It's an invitation," Nicole said, and then wondered where she had gotten that, whether it was true or something she wanted. She had not grown up with the tradition. Her grandmother had crossed at nineteen and raised children who raised children in a country where grief was supposed to be private, where you subjugated it to work schedules and casseroles and thank-you notes, and nobody built anything in the living room for the dead. Nicole had learned about Day of the Dead from a poster in Ms. Çelik's classroom last year, freshman Spanish, and had gone home and asked her grandmother about it, and her grandmother had laughed and said that was for other families, and changed the subject to whether Nicole was eating enough.

They got the bread, two loaves, still warm, and in the car the smell of orange peel and sugar filled everything, so that for ten blocks nobody spoke, which was not the bad kind of silence. Mustafa held the box on his lap like it was something he was responsible for now too.

It was when they carried the box inside that the twist arrived, in the form of the sideboard itself. Nicole's mother pulled the drawers out to clear the surface, and in the second drawer, under the good napkins, they found a bundle wrapped in a dish towel: sugar skulls, four of them, bought or made years ago, the icing gone chalky, and beneath them a photograph of Nicole's grandfather, who had died when Nicole was three, and a small square of paper in her grandmother's handwriting listing his favorite foods, tamales, café de olla, the sweet bread.

Neither of them said anything for a moment. Then Nicole's mother sat down on the arm of the couch, still holding the photograph, and Nicole understood that the denial she remembered, that's for other families, had been a lie or a door, and that her grandmother had been building an altar in secret for thirty years, in a drawer, with sugar skulls that had no one to be set out for.

"We can put them both up," Nicole said. "The photos together. The bread was both of theirs."

"It's old," her mother said of the skulls, but her thumb was moving over the photograph, and the stoic arrangement of her face had come apart at the mouth only, which was somehow worse and better than weeping.

"Ms. Çelik would say the old sugar counts double," Mustafa offered from the doorway, and Nicole laughed, an ugly startled sound, and her mother laughed too, briefly, and then cried a little, and then said the gratuitous thing, the thing Nicole would think about for weeks afterward: "I told her we didn't need all that. When I was young I told her it was superstitious. She never argued."

That evening they assembled the ofrenda together, photograph beside photograph, one loaf of the bread for each of them, and a cup of the coffee, and the four chalky skulls in front. Nicole stood looking at it and could not decide what she believed, whether any of this reached anyone, whether her grandmother knew, and she let herself not decide. Mustafa texted from home: send a picture. She took one, framed so the window behind it held the last of the daylight, and sent it, then set her phone face down on the sideboard next to the sugar.

"We'll get fresh ones next year," her mother said from the kitchen.

"Both days," Nicole said. "November first and second."

Her mother came and stood beside her, and put one of the sugar skulls into her hand.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2010 study claimed 'power poses' raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, but a larger 2015 replication found no such hormonal effect, though people still reported feeling more powerful.
story:
Maelle held her fork like a microphone and said, "My greatest weakness is that I care too much," and her mother winced before Mr. Fernando could.

He had come for dinner because he lived two floors down and because, after twenty years of hiring teenagers at the garden center, he had opinions. He set down his glass of water. "That is not a weakness. That is a compliment you are paying yourself. Try again."

The interview at Verdant Supply was Thursday at four. Maelle had applied because tuition deposits do not pay themselves, and because her mother had started saying things like, we'll manage, in a voice that meant they might not. Thursday was two days away, which was why dinner had turned into rehearsal, the lasagna cooling while Mr. Fernando leaned back in the good chair and pretended to be a manager named Dave.

"Tell me about yourself," he said.

She looked at the ceiling. She looked at her plate. She said, "I'm Maelle, I'm eighteen, I," and then the sentence went somewhere private and died.

"Eye contact," Mr. Fernando said, not unkindly. "Clear answers. Two things. That's all Dave wants."

That afternoon, before she'd come upstairs, she had stood in the restroom at the library with her hands on her hips and her chin lifted, feet apart, like a superhero waiting for a bus. Maia had sent her the idea with a string of flexed-arm emojis. Confidence, Maia had written. It's science. There's a study. Maelle had held the pose for two minutes, feeling mostly foolish, and then, because something in her resisted taking it on faith, she had looked it up.

The study was from 2010, and it had claimed that holding those expansive poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, the stress hormone. Maia hadn't mentioned that part, the hormones. Maia hadn't mentioned, either, the second thing Maelle found: a larger replication in 2015 that found no such hormonal effect at all. The one thing the replication did find was that people still reported feeling more powerful after the poses. Maelle had sat with that in the library's gray light, thumb hovering over the screen. Something in her had wanted the first study to be true, wanted a lever she could pull, chemistry she could boss around. Something else in her had felt almost relieved. If the feeling was all there was, then the feeling was up to her.

"You're somewhere else," her mother said, spooning more lasagna onto Mr. Fernando's plate whether he wanted it or not.

"I was thinking about a study," Maelle said. "Maia told me to do power poses before interviews. You stand like Wonder Woman and it changes your hormones. Except it doesn't. A bigger study tried it again and the hormones didn't move."

"Then it's nonsense," Mr. Fernando said.

"Not exactly. People still said they felt more powerful. That part held." She turned her fork over. "So it's not a lie, exactly. It's more like a trick you have to know is a trick."

Her mother said that sounded like most things, and Mr. Fernando laughed, and for a moment the dinner was easy again, and Maelle caught herself internalize, no, she caught herself believing it, the way you believe a thing you've turned over yourself rather than one handed to you whole. She wasn't sure the distinction was real. Maybe believing was believing. But the tested kind felt heavier, better balanced, like a chair you'd sat in rather than one you'd been told was sturdy.

"Again," Mr. Fernando said. "Tell me about yourself."

She looked at him this time, at the actual man and not the idea of a manager, and said, "I'm Maelle. I finished at St. Brigid's in June, I'm starting college in the fall, and I've been reading about which of our claims survive replication, because I'd rather be right than comfortable, though I'm not always successful at that." Her voice stayed level. Her eyes stayed where she'd put them.

Mr. Fernando set his fork down. "Hire you on the spot," he said. "That's not even germane to plants and I'd still hire you."

On Thursday she arrived at four, went to the restroom, and stood for two minutes with her hands on her hips, chin lifted, feeling the foolishness and, underneath it, something that might have been power or might have been the memory of choosing to stand that way. She didn't know which. She had decided, in the stall, that she could not know which, and that she would do it anyway, because feeling more powerful was feeling more powerful, whatever its pedigree. A woman at the sink watched her in the mirror and said, "You've got this, babe," and left before Maelle could answer.

The interview itself went the way weather goes, some of it clear and some of it not. She maintained eye contact with Dave, whose name really was Dave, through the questions about availability and teamwork. She gave clear answers. When he asked about customer service experience she said she didn't have any, and then said what she did have, which was a mother, a neighbor, and two years of fetching things for people who hadn't asked nicely. Dave wrote something down. She could not see what.

In the parking lot her phone buzzed. Maia: did you do the pose. Maelle typed back, yes, and it worked, and then deleted and it worked, and left it at yes. Then a second message arrived, from Maia again, and it had a photo attached, a screenshot of the Verdant Supply scheduling page, and in the corner of it, small but unmistakable, Maia's name on next Saturday's shift. Got the seasonal spot, the message said. apply for winter!! Maia had applied in March. Maia had never mentioned it.

Maelle stood between two parked cars with her phone warm in her hand, still carrying the residue of the pose in her shoulders, still not knowing whether the hormone claim or its failure mattered more to a girl who needed Saturday hours and a friend who got them first. Her phone buzzed a third time. Verdant Supply: thank you for interviewing, positions for the fall will post in August.

She put the phone in her pocket, unlocked her bike, and stood over it for a moment, hands on the handlebars, feet planted wide, before she rode home.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Electricity is billed by the kilowatt-hour, so using 600 kilowatt-hours at 15 cents each costs 90 dollars, before any fixed monthly charges.
story:
Jake had the two leases side by side on his knees in the molded plastic chair by the bank's front window, where the afternoon sun came through and turned the paper translucent. He was seventeen and had an appointment at the teller window in twenty minutes to set up his first checking account, but the real business of the afternoon was the paper in front of him: apartment A at 1,150 a month with heat included, apartment B at 985 with nothing included. He had a calculator app open and no idea which number to trust.

He had not expected choosing to feel like this. The listings had made it seem simple, one photograph of a sunlit kitchen after another, and now every page seemed to predicate its appeal on something hidden in the fine print. Apartment B looked cheaper by 165 dollars a month. He suspected it wasn't.

Maddex dropped into the chair beside him, smelling of the chlorine from morning swim practice, and peeled the cap off a fountain drink. "You look morose," Maddex said. "Worse than morose. You look like you're doing math."

"Utilities," Jake said. "B is cheaper but I pay electric, and the listing just says 'tenant pays utilities,' which tells me nothing. I don't even know what a month of electricity costs."

"You could ask," Maddex said, as if this were obvious, and turned his cup in his hands. Jake hated how obvious it was now that someone else had said it. He opened his messages and typed to Leana, who had interned at a property management office the summer before and knew the rituals.

The message he sent read: "Serious question. If I'm trying to budget for an apartment, how do I find out what the electric bill actually is? The listing won't say." He watched the typing dots appear and disappear twice before the answer came, and he read it under his breath: "Ask the landlord for the previous tenant's typical usage. They keep the records. Ask in kilowatt-hours, not dollars, because the rate can change but the usage won't. You do the math yourself." Below that, a second message: "Also, don't forget there's usually a fixed monthly charge on top. The kilowatt-hours aren't the whole bill."

Mr. Dela Cruz, in a gray suit with a lanyard reading COMMUNITY BANKING, came to the counter and called Jake's name. At the desk Jake pushed the leases across, because he wanted a witness to the arithmetic, someone whose job it was to look at numbers all day. The desk smelled of hand sanitizer and warm paper from the copier behind it. "I need to open an account," Jake said, "but first I need to know if I can afford this one."

Mr. Dela Cruz put on his glasses. "Then let's see what we're looking at."

The landlord of apartment B had answered an hour earlier: previous tenant averaged 600 kilowatt-hours a month, and the rate on the utility's plan was 15 cents per kilowatt-hour. Jake had the message open on his phone, the whole fact of it sitting there in blue bubbles. He did the multiplication on paper, slowly, because he wanted to watch it happen. Six hundred kilowatt-hours at fifteen cents each was ninety dollars. He wrote 90 and sat back. It felt strange that something so formless, all the lights and the refrigerator hum and the laptop chargers, could be counted out so exactly.

"So that's it," he said. "Ninety a month. Plus the 985. That's still cheaper than A by 75 dollars."

"Before any fixed monthly charges," Mr. Dela Cruz said, tapping Leana's message with one finger. "Your friend mentions them, and she's right to. You'd want to call the utility and ask what the fixed charge is. It won't be the ninety; it'll be more."

Jake felt the floor shift a little, not badly, just the way it did when a door you thought was locked turned out to open. He had done the arithmetic correctly, and it was still incomplete. The ninety dollars was true and it was not the whole truth, and both of those things could sit in the same hand. He added a blank line to his budget where the fixed charge would go and wrote, in small letters, "call before signing," and then made the same blank on the next page, because he still didn't know whether A's heat was really heat, or heat plus hot water, plus whatever else.

Mr. Dela Cruz slid the new debit card across the desk in its stiff paper sleeve and began the account paperwork, and Jake answered the questions, address of record, no address of record yet, while Maddex read the leases over his shoulder and said, "You know you're going to have to pick eventually." The fluorescent light buzzed faintly above the desk, and outside the window a woman was feeding a parking meter in the sun.

"I know," Jake said. "But not until I've called about the fixed charge. Both places. If B's still cheaper after that, I'll take B. If it's close, I'll take the one with heat included, because at least then I know the number." He squared the pages, folded them once, and put them in his backpack with the debit card still cool in his hand. "Can I use your phone?" he asked Maddex. "Mine's almost dead. I want to call the utility before they close."
